authors: ISTAT
title: Imprese e ICT. Anno 2025 (Statistica report)
population: Italian enterprises with >=10 persons employed, NACE Rev.2 C-N (excl. K) + S95.1 (Eurostat ICT-ENT scope); selection universe 218,446 enterprises
fieldwork_period: May-July 2025 (reference year 2025; some variables refer to 2024)
ai_definition: Use of at least one of 8 AI technologies (Eurostat ICT-ENT model questionnaire): text mining; speech recognition; natural language generation incl. code; image/video/audio generation (added 2025); image recognition/processing; machine learning for data analysis; AI-based RPA/decision support; autonomous physical movement of machines. Glossary: 'si riferisce a sistemi che utilizzano tecnologie per l'elaborazione di informazioni tratte da un testo non strutturato (text mining), il riconoscimento di immagini (computer vision), il riconoscimento vocale, la generazione del linguaggio naturale...'. Explicitly excludes 'le linee di produzione tradizionali e i sistemi di automazione generale che non includono componenti di intelligenza artificiale (ad esempio robot meccanici industriali)'. Aim: measure 'l'uso attivo e consapevole dell'IA'.
coi_note: Official statistics (EU-harmonised)
notes: Anchor source for RQ1. NACE C breakdown only for the headline AI indicator (14.7%); functions and barriers not published by sector in the report (sector data via Eurostat isoc_eb_ain2). Sample 26,246 enterprises, 17,041 usable respondents. 2025 adds image/video/audio generative AI to the technology list, a series break vs 2024 (ISTAT footnote). Page numbers = PDF pages. Data tables (xlsx) attached to the release extracted by scripts/extract_istat.py into data/istat/istat_ai_tables.csv.

authors: ISTAT
title: Imprese e ICT. Anno 2024 (Statistica report)

ai_definition: Use of at least one of 7 AI technologies (Eurostat ICT-ENT 2024; generative AI limited to natural language). Same exclusion of conventional automation as 2025.
coi_note: Official statistics
notes: Productivity-AI association is descriptive (turnover per employee quartiles), not causal. Key signal for RQ2: AI in production processes flat 2023-2024 while marketing/admin uses surged. Data tables (xlsx) attached to the release extracted by scripts/extract_istat.py into data/istat/istat_ai_tables.csv.

authors: ISTAT
title: Imprese e ICT. Anno 2023 (Statistica report)

coi_note: Official statistics
notes: Pre-generative-AI baseline: in 2023 AI use in Italian manufacturing was dominated by production uses (52.5% of manufacturing AI users). Compare with 2025 Eurostat data where production-process use is ~16% of manufacturing AI users (composition shift). 2022 comparison figure 6.2% (ISTAT) is from a different questionnaire year. Data tables (xlsx) attached to the release extracted by scripts/extract_istat.py into data/istat/istat_ai_tables.csv.

authors: ISTAT

authors: Eurostat
title: Artificial intelligence by size class of enterprise (isoc_eb_ai) and by NACE Rev. 2 activity (isoc_eb_ain2), ICT usage and e-commerce in enterprises survey
population: Enterprises with >=10 persons employed, NACE C-N excl. K + S95.1, EU27 and Member States
fieldwork_period: Survey years 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025 (dataset update 2026-06-15; extracted 2026-09-29 via Eurostat API)
ai_definition: E_AI_TANY: enterprises using at least one of AI_TTM (text mining), AI_TSR (speech recognition), AI_TNLG (NLG/speech synthesis/code), AI_TIR (image recognition), AI_TML (machine learning for data analysis), AI_TPA (AI-based RPA/decision support), AI_TAR (autonomous robots/vehicles/drones), E_AI_TPVSG (image/video/audio generation, from 2025).
coi_note: Official statistics
notes: Raw API extracts saved in sources/eurostat/*.json (isoc_eb_ai_TANY_bysize.json, isoc_eb_ain2_TANY_bynace.json, isoc_eb_ain2_C_allindic.json, isoc_eb_ai_IT_EU_2025_allindic.json). Barrier indicators E_AI_B* are expressed as % of ALL enterprises; divide by E_AI_EC for share among considerers (IT manufacturing 2025: lack of expertise 6.71/10.74 = 62%). 2021 values use a different technology list (break). Some IT subsector cells (C27_C28, C29_C30, C28) are missing for 2025 (confidentiality/reliability). Key RQ2 finding: Italian manufacturing AI growth 2023-2025 driven by text mining/genAI, while production-process AI stayed flat at ~2.3-2.6% of firms. Eurostat Statistics Explained page 'Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises' (Dec 2025) consulted for definitions and EU context.

authors: Eurostat
title: The use of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the European Union. Key results, 2026 edition
population: EU enterprises with >=10 persons employed (ICT-ENT) and individuals 16-74 (ICT-HH)
ai_definition: Same ICT-ENT AI technology list (8 technologies in 2025); purposes and reasons for non-use asked of users / considerers respectively.
coi_note: Official statistics

authors: Bencivelli, L.; Formai, S.; Mattevi, E.; Padellini, T.
title: Embracing the digital transition: the adoption of cloud computing and AI by Italian firms (Questioni di Economia e Finanza n. 946)
population: Italian firms with >=20 employees in industry excl. construction and non-financial private services (INVIND), plus Sondtel 2024
ai_definition: Self-reported use of AI (extensive, limited or experimental) in the firm's processes (INVIND module on advanced technologies); GenAI defined as 'the set of AI techniques for generating personalized responses to a user's requests (such as in the form of text, images or audio)'. Cloud treated as enabling prerequisite.
coi_note: Central bank research; views of authors
notes: Sector figure (INVIND sector groups, incl. food, chemicals, basic metals and engineering, textiles) available in charts only. Main reasons for adoption: 'upgrading of already automated production processes and the improvement of business support processes' (p.9). Positive correlation of AI adoption with realized and expected employment growth (linear regressions, correlational). Determinants: size, exports, group, MOPS management practices, R&D share. DOI resolves via doi.org to the PDF (not found in Crossref). Page numbers = PDF pages (printed page = PDF page - 2).

authors: Ropele, T.; Tagliabracci, A.
title: The economic impact of artificial intelligence: evidence from Italian firms (Questioni di Economia e Finanza n. 1005)
population: Italian firms with >=50 employees in industry and non-financial private services (SIGE survey, construction excluded from AI module), linked to Cerved CADS balance sheets and INPS employer-employee data
ai_definition: Question G1: 'How important is the use of artificial intelligence (e.g., cloud computing, predictive and/or generative artificial intelligence, robotics) to your company's activities?' Adopters = 'It is important and we are adopting it'. Very broad: includes cloud and robotics as examples.
coi_note: Central bank research; views of authors
notes: Quasi-causal (difference-in-differences) but self-selection possible; authors flag that parallel trends fail for blue-collar share and apprentices. Manufacturing firms less likely to state an opinion on AI than services (first-step logit, p.13). Very broad AI definition (includes cloud, robotics) inflates comparability issues vs ISTAT (RQ5). Printed DOI 10.32057/0.QEF.2026.1005 did not resolve at doi.org on 2026-09-30, so doi left null. SIGE waves ~1,500 firms (650 industry, 650 services, 200 construction).

authors: Bellomarini, L.; Bertolotti, F.; Citino, L.; Cassinis, M.G.; D'Amuri, F.; Del Prete, S.; Formai, S.; Mirenda, L.; Rigon, M.; Russo Russo, A.
title: L'adozione dell'intelligenza artificiale: effetti su produttivita e politiche a sostegno (Questioni di Economia e Finanza n. 1009)
population: Italian firms with >=20 employees (INVIND); balanced panel ~900 firms for DiD; Eurostat 10+ for barriers
geography: Italy (with EU/DE comparison and policy benchmarking incl. Singapore)
ai_definition: INVIND: use of AI tools (extensive, limited, experimental) in business processes; intensive use reported separately.
coi_note: Central bank research; views of authors
notes: Most recent and most policy-relevant BdI synthesis; contrasts null short-run firm-level effects (INVIND DiD, ~900 firms) with QEF 1005 positive DiD effects (SIGE, 50+ firms): key RQ4/RQ5 divergence. Discusses 'missing middle' in vertical AI supply for SMEs and non-selective subsidies; macro estimates from Bertolotti et al. (2026) are model-based projections. Page numbers = PDF pages.

authors: Bottone, M.; De Masi, L.; Mattevi, E.; Modugno, L.; Mongardini, M.

coi_note: Central bank statistics
notes: 'Industria' here = industry in the strict sense (manufacturing plus energy/extractive), not NACE C alone. Transizione 5.0 take-up 'rimasta invece piu contenuta, risentendo della scarsa conoscenza della misura' (p.5): qualitative only. Includes experimental use, so levels are much higher than ISTAT (RQ5). Sample size not stated in the note (INVIND ~4,000 firms).

authors: OECD

notes: Manufacturing-focused policy report; Italian box relies on IATI survey (University of Cagliari, IPSOS, Sapienza), n=200, representativeness not documented. Useful for barriers taxonomy (technological/operational, know-how, investment capacity).

coi_note: EU financial institution
notes: Different population (5+ employees), value-added weighting and definitions (AI bundled with big data; GenAI 'systematic use') produce much higher levels than ISTAT, but the Italy-EU gap persists (RQ5). authors: OECD
title: Progress in Implementing the European Union Coordinated Plan on Artificial Intelligence (Volume 1): Member States' Actions
population: EU Member States' AI policies (survey of and interviews with national authorities, document review); no firm-level data
geography: European Union, 27 Member States (Italy covered in country examples)
fieldwork_period: Member State survey and interviews 2024-2025; PDF generated October 2025, published 2026
ai_definition: Not applicable (policy stock-taking); AI uptake by firms discussed through national support programmes

Relevant to RQ3 (policy environment): Italy has no dedicated AI strategy budget (EUR 270 million per year estimated), relies on tax credits (Transition Plan 5.0, quoted at EUR 4.41 billion on p. 75 and EUR 6.3 billion on p. 110) and NRRP research funding (FAIR), and is one of three Member States with a net outflow of AI talent. Replaces the chapter-level record oecd2026cpaimanuf, which was a duplicate of oecd2026eucpai_v2 and was removed from the catalog.

authors: Ryseff, J.; De Bruhl, B.; Newberry, S. J.
title: The Root Causes of Failure for Artificial Intelligence Projects and How They Can Succeed: Avoiding the Anti-Patterns of AI
population: Experienced AI/ML practitioners (>=5 years experience): 50 industry data scientists/engineers recruited via LinkedIn (tech, health care, finance, retail, consulting, other; start-up to large firms) plus 15 academics from convenience samples
geography: Not stated; predominantly US (recruitment via LinkedIn, DoD-oriented study)
ai_definition: No adoption measure; an AI project failure is defined as 'a project that was perceived to be a failure by the organization', including both technical and business failures.
coi_note: Non-profit FFRDC research funded by NDRI exploratory research funds (DoD); no commercial vendor interest. Findings framed for U.S. DoD audience.
notes: Qualitative root-cause study (five anti-patterns: problem misunderstanding, lack of data, technology-first focus, inadequate infrastructure, problems too hard for AI). Relevant to RQ3 (barriers: leadership, data, infrastructure). Critical note: the widely quoted '>80% of AI projects fail' is NOT a RAND measurement but a secondary estimate cited from a press article (Kahn, fn 13) and is often misattributed to RAND in grey literature. No manufacturing, Italian or European coverage; interviewees are technical staff (supply-side view), sample small and self-selected (13.2% acceptance). Useful for triangulating barriers, not for prevalence.

authors: Singla, A.; Sukharevsky, A.; Yee, L.; Chui, M.; Hall, B.; Balakrishnan, T.
title: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation
population: Online panel respondents 'at all levels of the organization' across regions, industries, company sizes; 38% from organizations with >USD 1 billion revenue; advanced manufacturing subsample n=136
geography: Global, 105 nations; no country breakdown published (Italy not identifiable)
ai_definition: Respondent-reported 'regular use' of AI (incl. gen AI) in at least one of 11 business functions; maturity self-classified as experimenting, piloting, scaling, fully scaled; AI agents defined as 'systems based on foundation models capable of acting in the real world, planning and executing multiple steps in a workflow'.
coi_note: Published by McKinsey's AI consultancy arm (QuantumBlack), which sells AI transformation services; report promotes 'high performer' practices (workflow redesign, scaling) that map onto its service offering.
notes: Most-cited global benchmark; strong upward bias versus official statistics (88% 'use' vs ~8-13% of EU enterprises in Eurostat), explained by opt-in online panel of self-selected respondents, overrepresentation of large firms (38% >USD 1bn revenue), function-level 'regular use' definition and GDP-weighting. No country results; Italy not identifiable. Manufacturing is both a business function and an industry (advanced manufacturing n=136); the p.10 industry column mapping is inferred from the footnote order and sorted totals (86% for advanced manufacturing). Useful for RQ5 (definitional divergence: breadth vs scaling vs EBIT impact) and depth metrics. Trend n: 2021 n=1,843; 2022 1,492; 2023 1,684; Feb-Mar 2024 1,363; Jul 2024 1,491 (p.9). PDF retrieved via Internet Archive (web.archive.org) because mckinsey.com blocks automated access; landing page https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai could not be fetched.

authors: Deloitte AI Institute
title: State of AI in the Enterprise (2026 edition)
population: Director-level to board/C-suite leaders (split equally IT and line-of-business) directly involved in AI strategy/implementation, at organizations that ALREADY have one or more working AI implementations used daily; six industries
geography: 24 countries; Italy n=75 (2.3% of sample); US n=1,200; Germany n=170; France n=150; Spain n=100; EMEA n=1,170
ai_definition: Not an adoption rate: all respondents' organizations are screened in as already using AI ('All participating organizations have one or more working implementations of AI being used daily'); depth measured as share of AI experiments moved to production, degree of business transformation, agentic and physical AI use (self-rated extent).
coi_note: Deloitte sells AI strategy, implementation and managed services; report concludes with 'critical actions for leaders' aligned to its offerings; no disclosure of panel provider, response rate or weighting.
notes: Key methodological red flag: sample restricted to organizations already using AI daily (selection on the outcome), so no prevalence estimate is possible and all shares describe adopters only. Italy only n=75 and not reported separately. Respondents are AI-involved senior leaders (optimism and social desirability bias). Figure 10 label 'Americas N=3,235' appears to be a labelling error (regional n not fully reported). Useful for RQ1 depth (pilot-to-production gap), RQ3 (skills as top barrier) and RQ5 (definitions: adopters-only frame).

authors: Deloitte AI Institute
title: State of AI in the Energy, Resources, and Industrials Industry
population: Energy, resources and industrials (ER&I, incl. industrial products/manufacturing) subsample of the State of AI in the Enterprise 2026 survey: director to C-suite leaders at organizations already using AI daily
geography: 24 countries (Italy n=75 in total sample; ER&I country split not reported)
ai_definition: As in the parent survey: adopters only; depth indicators (share of experiments in production, transformation level, agentic and physical AI use extent).
coi_note: Deloitte industry marketing report derived from its commercial survey; Deloitte sells AI and industrial transformation services.
notes: Closest Deloitte proxy for manufacturing, but ER&I mixes energy, mining, utilities, chemicals and industrial products; manufacturing not isolated; no Italian breakdown. Adopters-only sample (see deloitte2026stateai). 'Physical AI' (robotics, automated machinery) conflates conventional industrial automation with AI, inflating the 72% figure: key definitional issue for RQ5.

authors: Michalski, J.; Winters, S.; Gunn, D.; Holland, J.
title: AI ROI: The paradox of rising investment and elusive returns
population: Senior executives with decision or oversight role in AI strategy/investment at organizations with one or more working AI implementations in daily use (and gen AI pilots or implementations)
geography: 14 countries in Europe and Middle East: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Norway, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Sweden, Switzerland, Netherlands, UAE, UK (country n not reported); 24 interviews in FR, DE, NL, UK
ai_definition: Adopters only: 'All organizations have one or more working implementations of AI in daily use'; ROI measured as self-reported time to satisfactory return on a typical AI use case.
coi_note: Deloitte thought-leadership piece concluding that value requires CEO-led, organization-wide transformation programmes, i.e. the consulting services Deloitte sells; methodology section notes internal gen AI platform was used in analysis.
notes: Only European consultancy source directly on AI ROI; qualitative interview findings on why ROI is hard to measure (intangible benefits, siloed data, AI entangled with broader transformation) are useful for RQ4 and for explaining weak self-reported ROI. Adopters-only sample; Italy included but country n and industry split not reported; ROI is self-assessed payback, not measured. Quote wording in global page uses both 'per cent' and 'percent'. Italian translation page also available.

authors: Deloitte Italy (press office)
title: Deloitte: adozione dell'intelligenza artificiale a un punto cruciale, le aziende si avvicinano alla fase di piena integrazione (State of AI in the Enterprise 2026, Italian results)
population: Italian respondents to Deloitte State of AI in the Enterprise 2026: director to C-suite leaders at organizations already using AI daily (Italy n=75 according to global methodology, p.40 of deloitte2026stateai)
ai_definition: Adopters only (screened on having working AI implementations in daily use); gen AI and agentic AI use self-reported.
coi_note: Press release by Deloitte Italy promoting its report and services; closes with a call to rethink processes around AI or 'lose ground' to AI-native firms.
notes: Only Italy-specific cut of a major consultancy AI survey found, but based on n=75 (not disclosed in the press release; taken from global methodology) adopters-only respondents, no sector split, no confidence intervals. Internal inconsistency red flag: agentic AI use (~70%) reported higher than gen AI use (62%), implausible given agentic systems are built on gen AI, suggesting loose definitions or question wording effects. 'Only 35% have calculated ROI' is a useful RQ4 data point on the weakness of self-reported ROI evidence.

authors: Lussu, F.; Deep, A.; Fojan, C.
title: AI in Manufacturing 2026: From pilots to scale. Maturity, impact, barriers, and trends
population: Manufacturing organizations (metals/forging/casting, medical devices, automotive, industrial machinery, battery, aerospace, electronics, chemicals, pharma, food and beverage); majority of responses from senior decision-makers; recruitment method not stated
geography: Europe excl. Germany 43%, Asian 'giants' 33%, Germany 14%, United States 10%; no Italy breakdown
ai_definition: Not formally defined; AI technologies grouped as machine learning/deep learning, gen AI and agentic AI, and physical AI/closed-loop; value is self-reported 'measurable value' and 'improvement potential' on operational KPIs.
coi_note: Deloitte consulting marketing study ('what leaders should do next'); recommends scaling pipelines, governance and deployment models that Deloitte provides.
notes: One of few consultancy surveys focused only on manufacturing and on shop-floor use cases (quality, production, maintenance), useful for RQ2 and RQ3. Red flags: small convenience-type sample (140+), recruitment and fieldwork dates not disclosed, no Italian breakdown (Europe excl. Germany 43%), impact is 'improvement potential' (expected) rather than measured, and the web page and PDF slightly differ (PDF: Quality+Production ~61% of use cases; web: Quality 62%). Barrier ranking (cost first, then skills, change resistance) is consistent with Istat/Eurostat barrier items for Italian firms.

org: Deloitte Insights (Deloitte Consulting LLP) with the Manufacturing Leadership Council
authors: Gaus, T.; Schlotterbeck, M.
title: 2025 Smart Manufacturing and Operations Survey: Navigating challenges to implementation
population: Executives of manufacturing and operations companies with annual revenue >= USD 500 million, >1,000 employees, HQ or operations in the US (consumer products, industrial products, energy and chemicals, mining and metals, automotive, aviation, life sciences, technology)
ai_definition: Use of AI/machine learning and generative AI 'at the facility or network level' (scaled) versus piloting, self-reported.
coi_note: Authored by Deloitte Consulting's smart manufacturing practice leaders; survey supports the case for smart manufacturing investment which Deloitte sells.
notes: US large-firm benchmark only (>=USD 500m revenue, >1,000 employees), useful as an upper-bound comparator for depth of AI in factories: even among very large US manufacturers only 29% use AI/ML at facility or network scale. Impact figures refer to smart manufacturing overall (not AI) and are self-reported. Not relevant to Italian SMEs directly; include for RQ5 contrast (population differences).

authors: Johansson, S.; Madgavkar, A.; Schrader, U.; Ramirez, M. J.; Rigby, X.
title: Agents, robots, and us: How AI reshapes work and skills in Europe
population: Workforce (occupations, work activities, ~3,900 skills) in 10 European countries incl. Italy; job postings (Lightcast) 2023-2025
geography: Czech Republic, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom (Italy country dashboard pp.53-57 printed, PDF pp.55-59)
fieldwork_period: Employment and wages 2024; job postings 2023 to Q4 2025; projections to 2030
ai_definition: Technical automation potential of work activities (share of work hours automatable with existing technology, expert assessment) and modelled adoption scenarios to 2030; AI skills demand measured from job postings mentioning AI fluency or technical AI skills.
coi_note: MGI is McKinsey's research arm (states editorial independence) but the parent firm sells AI and automation transformation; 'value unlocked' figures are wage-bill-based potentials that support the business case for adoption.
notes: Not an adoption measure: potentials and scenario projections (automation adoption x FTE x 2024 wages), highly assumption-dependent. Useful for RQ1/RQ4 context (Italy's high manufacturing exposure: USD 52bn of 196bn) and for skills-demand evidence from job postings (Italy: demand for AI fluency doubled since 2023, 'less than the regional average'). Uses Istat, Eurostat, Lightcast and O*NET inputs. Red flag for RQ5: 'value unlocked' is a wage-bill potential and is often misread as realized productivity gain. PDF retrieved via Internet Archive; McKinsey landing page https://www.mckinsey.com/mgi/our-research/agents-robots-and-us-how-ai-reshapes-work-and-skills-in-europe not fetched directly.

org: World Economic Forum (in collaboration with McKinsey & Company)
authors: World Economic Forum
title: Global Lighthouse Network: The Mindset Shifts Driving Impact and Scale in Digital Transformation (White Paper)
population: 189 'Lighthouse' factories, sustainability sites and value chains selected by WEF/McKinsey assessment (36 new in 2024); top-5 use cases presented for designation
geography: 33 countries, 35 subsectors (no Italian site among 2024 cohorts)
ai_definition: Share of each Lighthouse's top-five use cases enabled by 'analytical AI' or 'generative AI' as presented during site evaluation.
coi_note: GLN is co-run with McKinsey & Company as knowledge partner, which conducts the assessments and sells operations transformation; industrial partners (Schneider Electric, Siemens, Aramco) are technology vendors. Showcase format.
notes: Extreme positive selection: sites are chosen because they achieved step-change results (survivorship), impacts are self-reported by applicants and validated by the consultancy running the programme; no counterfactual. Useful as frontier benchmark for RQ2 (use-case domains: quality, asset management, planning) and for RQ5 contrast between frontier cases and population statistics. No Italian site in the 2024 cohorts.

org: World Economic Forum (in collaboration with McKinsey & Company)
authors: World Economic Forum
title: Global Lighthouse Network: Rewiring Operations for Resilience and Impact at Scale (White Paper)
population: 223 Lighthouse sites (factories and value chains) selected by WEF/McKinsey; 2025 cohorts
geography: >30 countries, 40 industries; no Italian site mentioned in the report
ai_definition: Share of top-five use cases embedding analytical AI/machine learning or gen AI.
coi_note: Foreword co-signed by McKinsey, Siemens, Schneider Electric, Aramco Ventures, Beko, Foxconn Industrial Internet: vendors and consultancy with commercial interest in industrial AI.
notes: Same selection-on-success caveat as wef2025gln. Even the frontier sample reports that enterprise-wide scaling is rare, which corroborates the pilot-to-scale gap in survey evidence (RQ1 depth). Italy absent from recent cohorts; Italian presence in GLN limited to early cohorts (see wef2019beacons).

org: World Economic Forum (in collaboration with McKinsey & Company)
authors: World Economic Forum
title: Fourth Industrial Revolution: Beacons of Technology and Innovation in Manufacturing (White Paper)
population: First cohorts of Lighthouse factories (16 initial sites plus new ones) selected from >1,000 screened sites; includes two Italian sites: Rold (Cerro Maggiore, SME) and Bayer Division Pharmaceuticals (Garbagnate)
geography: Global; Italian cases Rold Cerro Maggiore and Bayer Garbagnate
ai_definition: Fourth Industrial Revolution (4IR) technologies broadly (IIoT, dashboards, additive manufacturing, analytics, AI); not AI-specific.
coi_note: Co-produced with McKinsey & Company; showcase of selected best-practice sites.
notes: Only Italian lighthouse cases found in GLN reports (Rold SME and Bayer Garbagnate pharma plant). Relevant for RQ5: flagship 'Industry 4.0' Italian cases are IoT/OEE digitalisation rather than AI proper, illustrating definitional slippage between 4IR/Industria 4.0 and AI in grey literature. Rold case also documents enablers typical of Italian SMEs (university partnerships, change management, vendor collaboration) for RQ3. Revenue impact is self-reported and not causal.

org: The European House - Ambrosetti (with Microsoft Italia)
authors: The European House - Ambrosetti
title: AI 4 Italy: Impacts and Prospects of Generative Artificial Intelligence for Italy and Made in Italy
population: Survey of 'more than 100' Italian companies from the TEHA network (InnoTech Community members and heads of companies) plus stakeholder interviews; macro impact model for the Italian economy
fieldwork_period: 2023 (before 1 September 2023 presentation at Cernobbio Forum; exact dates not stated)
ai_definition: Generative AI; firm-level use = 'have already tried using AI solutions'; macro impact = upper-bound added value from extensive gen AI adoption at constant hours worked.
coi_note: Commissioned/co-produced with Microsoft Italia, a leading gen AI vendor (Copilot, Azure OpenAI); presented with Microsoft Italia CEO. Strong incentive to emphasise upside.
notes: Highly cited in Italian policy debate ('+18% GDP'). Red flags: the 18% is explicitly an upper limit of a task-exposure model, not a forecast; firm survey (100+ companies) is a convenience sample of TEHA's network of large, innovation-oriented firms, so '1 in 2 have tried AI' is not comparable with Istat (about 8% of firms >=10 employees in 2024). Full PDF not located; figures verified on the publisher's English page.

org: Minsait (Indra Group) and The European House - Ambrosetti
authors: Minsait; The European House - Ambrosetti
title: Lo stato dell'arte dell'Intelligenza Artificiale nelle aziende italiane: Adozione, impatti e prospettive (Artificial Intelligence in Italy 2025: Adoption, Impacts and Prospects)
population: 284 Italian companies with more than 249 employees, several sectors (manufacturing 28.8%), 80% of respondents top management; opt-in TEHA network survey, fieldwork 2024-25
fieldwork_period: Not stated (published 8 May 2025, presented at TEHA Technology Forum 2025, Stresa)
ai_definition: Self-reported adoption stage: already adopted/experimenting, planning to adopt, extended implementation at company scale, no intention; productivity impact self-assessed as % gain.
coi_note: Minsait is an IT consulting and systems integration firm selling AI solutions; TEHA is a consultancy/think tank; no disclosure of sampling frame, response rate or sector weights.
notes: Full PDF (72 pp., May 2025) provided by the author on 2026-10-01; all figures re-verified against it, page references added. Earlier values taken from trade press are confirmed. Caveats: '63% adopted or intend to adopt' merges adopters (38.2%) and planners (25.2%); opt-in sample of large firms (>249 employees).

authors: de Bellefonds, N.; Charanya, T.; Franke, M. R.; Apotheker, J.; Forth, P.; Grebe, M.; Luther, A.; de Laubier, R.; Lukic, V.; Martin, M.; Nopp, C.; Sassine, J.
title: Where's the Value in AI?
population: CxOs and senior executives across >20 sectors and 10 industries (incl. industrial goods, 'machines and automation', automotive, chemicals)
geography: 59 countries in Asia, Europe and North America (country split not reported)
fieldwork_period: 2024 (BCG Build for the Future 2024 Global Study merged with Digital Acceleration Index; exact dates not stated)
ai_definition: Composite AI maturity score from self-assessment of 30 'enterprise foundational capabilities' (four maturity stages each), weighted by contribution to self-reported AI value; firms classified as AI stagnating, emerging, scaling, future-built.
coi_note: BCG sells AI transformation; the '70-20-10' (people-technology-algorithms) resource rule is a BCG proprietary framework that the survey is said to 'confirm'; maturity score is built on BCG's own capability model.
notes: Widely cited '74% see no tangible value / 4% substantial value'. Red flags: maturity categories are constructed from self-assessed capabilities weighted by self-reported value (circularity); no country or firm-size breakdown; sampling frame and response rate undisclosed; the 70-20-10 split is BCG experience 'corroborated' by the survey rather than a measured quantity. Manufacturing proxies: machines and automation, automotive, chemicals (Exhibit 4). Useful for RQ1 depth, RQ3 barriers (ROI, prioritisation, security) and RQ5. Landing page and PDF (https://web-assets.bcg.com/a5/37/be4ddf26420e95aa7107a35aae8d/bcg-wheres-the-value-in-ai.pdf) retrieved via Internet Archive; bcg.com blocks automated access.

authors: Boston Consulting Group
title: AI at Work 2025: Momentum Builds, But Gaps Remain (third edition, slideshow)
population: Individual employees: one-third each frontline white-collar employees (no managerial responsibility), managers and leaders, across industries incl. manufacturing and company sizes (<USD 500m to >USD 5bn revenue)
geography: 11 countries/regions; Italy n=1,011; also India, Brazil, UK, France, Japan, Spain, Germany, US, Middle East (Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE), South Africa (n=509)
fieldwork_period: 2025 (published June 2025; fieldwork dates not stated in slideshow)
ai_definition: Individual-level use of AI/gen AI tools 'at least several times a week' (regular use); company-level items reported by employees (workflow redesign, integration of AI agents).
coi_note: BCG sells AI and workforce transformation; results framed to promote workflow redesign ('Reshape') and training programmes.
notes: One of few commercial surveys with a sizeable Italian sample (n=1,011), but it measures individual white-collar employees' use, not firm adoption, and oversamples leaders/managers (2/3 of sample) and large firms. Italian regular use (68%) is incompatible in level with Istat firm-level adoption (~8% of firms in 2024) and illustrates the unit-of-analysis divergence central to RQ5. Frontline regular use stalled at 51% (52% in 2024) versus 78% managers and 85-88% leaders (p.6). Country ordering mapped from chart labels (values sorted descending). PDF retrieved via Internet Archive copy of this URL; bcg.com landing page (https://www.bcg.com/publications/2025/ai-at-work-momentum-builds-but-gaps-remain) blocked automated access.

authors: EY
title: EY European AI Barometer 2025. From concerns to confidence: The workforce's response to AI
population: Managers and non-executive employees across 21 sectors (incl. advanced manufacturing, industrial products) in 9 European countries; plus social-media listening (41 million AI conversations 2024)
geography: 9 European countries: Switzerland, Spain, Germany, Portugal, Italy (n=539), Netherlands, Belgium, France, Austria
ai_definition: Individual respondents 'ever involved with or actively used' AI (e.g. ChatGPT, Perplexity, Midjourney); use of AI tools at work; organisational financial effects as perceived by respondents.
coi_note: EY sells AI advisory (EY.ai); the report ends with investment recommendations and collaboration with 'AI specialists'.
notes: Individual-level perception survey; the 56% 'financial benefits' is employee/manager perception of organisational effects, not measured financials. Striking management vs employee perception gap (57% vs 35%) is useful evidence on self-report bias for RQ4/RQ5: exec-only surveys (McKinsey, Deloitte) likely overstate impact. Sampling method undisclosed. Italy-specific results in ey2025italybarometer.

authors: EY Italy (press office)
title: EY Italy AI Barometer, cresce l'adozione dell'intelligenza artificiale nelle aziende italiane: +34% nell'ultimo anno (press release, 5 August 2025)
population: Italian professionals (managers and employees) of companies in various sectors, subsample of EY European AI Barometer 2025
ai_definition: Individual respondents declaring use of AI tools at work.
coi_note: EY Italy press release quoting its AI & Data partner; promotional framing.
notes: Red flags: headline '+34%' is actually a +34 percentage-point change (12% to 46%), a near quadrupling that is implausible for a representative panel and suggests sample or question changes between waves; no sector split and no sampling details. Individual-level measure, not firm adoption; not comparable with Istat enterprise statistics. Full Italian report is behind a download form (not accessed).

authors: PwC Italia
title: 29th Annual Global & Italian CEO Survey: I CEO italiani restano ottimisti e puntano sulla crescita, ma i ritardi nell'adozione dell'IA frenano la competitività
population: CEOs (all industries) worldwide; Italian subsample of 118 CEOs
ai_definition: CEO-reported extent of AI implementation across business areas (demand generation, support services, product/service development, strategic direction, demand fulfilment), with 'little or no implementation' as the reported category; AI financial benefits = CEO-reported revenue increase and/or cost reduction.
coi_note: PwC sells AI and business model reinvention services; the survey is also a marketing flagship presented at Davos. Less directly promotional of AI than vendor-sponsored studies (reports that 56% see no impact).
notes: Strong Italy vs world comparison from the same instrument (useful for RQ1 and RQ3: Italian CEOs report little or no AI implementation more often than global peers in every area analysed; culture, roadmap and skills gaps larger than global). Limitations: Italian n=118 CEOs, no sector split in the Italian release, single informant (CEO), CEO sampling frame skewed to larger firms. Global PDF report not downloaded; press coverage citing '78% of Italian CEOs report no benefits' was not found in the PwC page and is therefore not recorded.

authors: Capgemini Research Institute
title: Harnessing the value of AI: Unlocking scalable, agentic AI (Generative AI in organizations 2025, research brief)
population: Director-level and above executives at organizations with annual revenue > USD 1 billion, 11 sectors incl. manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and defense
geography: 15 countries incl. Italy (about 5% of organizations by HQ country, p.64); Australia, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, India, Japan, Netherlands, Norway, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, UK, US
ai_definition: Self-reported gen AI maturity stage: exploring potential; pilots; enabled in some functions/locations; enabled in most/all functions/locations ('adoption' = partially or fully enabled). AI agents: implemented at partial or full scale.
coi_note: Capgemini is an IT services and AI integrator; the research institute's reports support its consulting and 'platformization' offerings.
notes: Large-firm (>USD 1bn) sample only; Italy about 5% (roughly 55 organizations) and not reported separately. Report itself warns findings 'are intended to provide directional guidance'. Manufacturing values read from the stacked-bar chart image (p.10), base n=1,020 organizations at least exploring gen AI. Useful for RQ1 depth: even among large manufacturers only about 21% have enabled gen AI beyond pilots. Related Capgemini-Microsoft whitepaper 'The New AI Imperative in Manufacturing' (2025) was screened and excluded (no survey, vendor claims).

authors: Microsoft AI Economy Institute
title: Global AI Adoption in 2025: A Widening Digital Divide (AI Diffusion Report H2 2025)
population: Working-age population by country (individual users of generative AI products)
geography: Global, country ranking incl. Italy, Germany, France, Spain, Poland, UK
ai_definition: 'AI diffusion' = share of people (working-age) who used a generative AI product during the period, derived from aggregated anonymised Microsoft telemetry adjusted for OS/device market share, internet penetration and population.
coi_note: Microsoft is a leading gen AI vendor (Copilot, Azure OpenAI) and the metric is derived from its own telemetry; incentive to document growing diffusion.
notes: Population-level individual usage indicator (not firm adoption, not manufacturing). Useful for RQ5 as context: Italy's individual gen AI diffusion (27.8%) is similar to Germany and Poland but well below France and Spain, whereas Italian firm-level AI adoption (Istat/Eurostat) lags more markedly; the metric depends on Microsoft's device share corrections (see technical paper). Contains no manufacturing breakdown.

authors: Bencivelli, L.; De Masi, L.; Falck, E.; Fernandez Cerezo, A.; Formai, S.; Hidalgo Bricio, I.; Mattevi, E.; Nagengast, A.
title: Embracing AI in Europe: New evidence from harmonised central bank business surveys
population: Private non-financial firms with >=20 employees in industry excl. construction and non-financial private services (harmonised Bundesbank BOP-F, Banca d'Italia INVIND, Banco de Espana EBAE)
fieldwork_period: Italy INVIND Feb-May 2024 and Feb-May 2025; Germany BOP-F Apr-Jun 2024 and Apr-Jun 2025; Spain EBAE Nov 2024
ai_definition: Common questionnaire: use of AI (predictive or generative) and gen AI by intensity (intensive, limited, experimental); weighted with firm weights.
coi_note: Central bank economists writing in a personal capacity; no commercial interest.
notes: Highest-quality cross-country comparator found in this layer: harmonised, representative, weighted surveys that place Italy far behind Germany and Spain in 2024 but with fast catch-up in gen AI (5% to 24%), while intensive use is under 4% everywhere (depth gap, RQ1). Direct evidence that Italian manufacturing lags services in gen AI adoption. Complementarities with cloud and robotics and path dependence from early experimentation are relevant to RQ3. Overlaps with Banca d'Italia QEF 946 (institutional layer). Author list taken from search index (the archived page did not render the byline); publication date early 2026 (mirror dated 2 February 2026); verify byline before citing. Numbers verified on the archived CEPR page (live page blocked by Cloudflare).

authors: Bick, A.; Blandin, A.; Deming, D. J.; Fuchs-Schundeln, N.; Jessen, J.
title: Differences in AI adoption in Europe and the US: Explanations and implications for productivity growth
population: (1) Workers in 7 countries (France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, UK, US) surveyed May-June 2025 and Jan-Feb 2026 (Real-Time Population Survey design); (2) firms in 32 European countries from Eurostat ICT usage in enterprises survey 2021-2025
geography: France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, UK, US (workers); 32 European countries (firms)
fieldwork_period: Worker survey January-February 2026 (N=20,916) and May-June 2025; EU ICT survey 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025
ai_definition: Workers: use of generative AI for work and share of weekly work hours spent using it; firms: use of at least one of eight specified AI technologies (Eurostat definition).
coi_note: Academic economists (CEPR Discussion Paper 21337, 'Mind the gap: AI adoption in Europe and the US'); no commercial sponsor identified.
notes: Italy has the lowest worker gen AI adoption among the 7 countries (26%), and low intensity; management practices and employer encouragement explain most of the gap, a key RQ3 enabler finding. Productivity estimates are correlational at country-industry level (with placebo checks), not causal. Byline of the column not rendered in the archived page; authors taken from the underlying CEPR DP cited in the column (Bick et al. 2026). Live page blocked by Cloudflare; figures verified on archived copy.

authors: Aldasoro, I.; Gambacorta, L.; Pal, R.; Revoltella, D.; Weiss, C.; Wolski, M.
title: How AI is affecting productivity and jobs in Europe
population: More than 12,000 EU firms in the European Investment Bank Investment Survey (EIBIS 2019-2024) matched to Orbis balance sheets, with matched US firms for identification
geography: EU27 (country groups by financial development) and US
ai_definition: EIBIS firm-reported use of big data analytics and AI; instrument = AI adoption rate of matched US firms (sector, size, investment, innovation, financing, management).
coi_note: Authors from BIS and EIB (public institutions) writing in personal capacity; CEPR Discussion Paper No. 21082.
notes: Best causal RQ4 evidence in this layer (IV design), EU-wide incl. Italy but no Italy-specific estimate in the column. EIBIS 'big data analytics and AI' definition is broader than Eurostat AI, so adoption levels (24-45%) are not comparable with Istat/Eurostat. Relevance for Italy: SME-dominated structure implies smaller gains; training complementarity (5.9pp) supports RQ3 skills findings. Byline not rendered in archive; authors taken from the DP reference in the column.

authors: Hoffmann, M.; Nurski, L.
title: What is holding back artificial intelligence adoption in Europe? (Policy Contribution 24/2021)
population: Secondary analysis of EU enterprise surveys: Eurostat ICT usage in enterprises 2020/2021 (~142,000 firms) and European Commission (2020) survey on AI adoption (9,640 firms)
ai_definition: Compares definitions: Eurostat (four AI types incl. ML and NLP on big data, chatbots, service robots) vs European Commission 2020 taxonomy (10 AI application types).
coi_note: Independent think tank; project funded by the Mastercard Center for Inclusive Growth (disclosed), no direct commercial interest in AI adoption figures.
notes: Key methodological anchor for RQ5: shows that non-response bias (7% response) and taxonomy differences explain a sixfold gap between two institutional EU estimates, directly applicable to the appraisal of consulting surveys with undisclosed response rates. Manufacturing uses AI mainly in production/process applications (robots, process automation, equipment optimisation), relevant to RQ2. Table 2 column order: all sectors, agriculture, manufacturing, construction/utilities, trade/transport, IT/finance/real estate, education/health (manufacturing = third value). Older (2021) but conceptually central.

authors: Accenture
title: Accenture: le aziende europee devono accelerare l'adozione dell'Intelligenza Artificiale per colmare il divario di produttività (press release on the study 'Europe's AI Reckoning', 1 July 2025)
population: 800 large European companies (study focus on firms with revenue > EUR 1 billion); sectors incl. automotive, aerospace and defense, industrial, telecom, utilities; Italian subsample size not disclosed
geography: Europe incl. Italy, Switzerland, Germany, UK, France, Spain
fieldwork_period: Not stated in the press release (secondary coverage reports July 2024 to February 2025)

Method: probit AMEs plus propensity score matching; correlational (authors acknowledge endogeneity not fully ruled out). Key determinants: prior IoT/big data/AR and robotics, firm size, employee welfare services; AI training linked only to information technologies. Internal inconsistency on fiscal incentives: the introduction says the incentive association with AI adoption disappears in the matched sample, whereas Table 6 and Section 4.2 report tax incentive AMEs significant in matched columns 4-5 (0.046***, 0.020**) and weakly (10%) in the full sample; abstract/conclusion say incentives support adoption only among already digitalized firms. In industry (matched) tax incentives correlate with AI adoption (0.011*), not in services. Important for RQ5: RIL measures AI investment (1.3%) vs ISTAT AI use (~6.4%).

authors: Shah, Syed Muhammad Ali; Cincera, Michele; Cucculelli, Marco
title: The bright and dark sides of AI-driven transformation: evidence from Italian firms
population: Italian micro, small and medium-sized enterprises in manufacturing, services and utilities (sampling frame of 64,872 MSMEs from Bureau van Dijk Orbis/AIDA); no sector breakdown reported
fieldwork_period: Survey May 2019 to February 2020; AI adoption tracked via LinkedIn profiles 2020-2023; performance from AIDA/Orbis t to t+4
ai_definition: Two measures. (1) AI Capability Index: factor-analytic composite of survey items on tangible (data generation and sources, technologies such as IoT, analytics, cloud, robots), human (employment of data analysts, data scientists, CDOs; data use in decisions) and intangible (coordination, change capacity, risk proclivity) knowledge, each pillar rescaled 0-1 and averaged. (2) AI adoption: binary = firm employed at least one individual with AI-specific skills on LinkedIn between 2020 and 2023 (BERT skill classifier).
coi_note: Academic authors (UNIVPM Ancona, ULB Brussels); CC BY open access; no commercial interest identified.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Links a 2019-2020 survey of 6,732 Italian MSMEs (manufacturing, services, utilities; frame 64,872 firms from Orbis/AIDA; survey design described in Cucculelli et al. 2024) to LinkedIn skill data 2020-2023 and AIDA balance sheets, estimating a two-stage CDM-inspired model (probit for innovation, OLS for productivity) with 2-digit ATECO and region fixed effects. AI is measured on its own and separately from the Industry 4.0 bundle, but in two indirect ways: an AI Capability Index (factor composite of data, technology, skills and organisational items, mean 0.17 on 0-1) and a binary adoption proxy (at least one AI-skilled employee on LinkedIn, 8.1% of firms), which the authors themselves read as capability or path dependence rather than deployed AI; no manufacturing-specific estimate is reported although manufacturing is in the frame. Limitations: non-causal (authors explicit), cross-sectional capabilities, LinkedIn undercoverage of micro firms, modest pillar reliabilities (alpha 0.61-0.74). Relevance: RQ1 (8.1% talent-based adoption proxy for Italian MSMEs, no sector split), RQ3 (prior capabilities and government support as enablers; capability-contingent policy effects), RQ4 (innovation-productivity associations, green innovation persistent over four years, brown short-run), RQ5 (contrast between talent/capability proxies and Istat use-based definitions).

authors: Montresor, Sandro; Vezzani, Antonio
title: Digital technologies and eco-innovation. Evidence of the twin transition from Italian firms

coi_note: Academic authors (GSSI, Roma Tre); no commercial interest.
notes: Version read: accepted author manuscript from IRIS UniTN (own pagination 1-29); version of record Industry and Innovation 30(7):766-800 not read (T&F 403). Data: ISTAT Permanent Census of Firms 2019 (~200k firms surveyed, 154,782 usable). Heckman-type probit with sample selection (eco-action); authors state "we can hardly claim for causality". No sector-specific results (70 industry fixed effects; manufacturing not separated). Key caveat for RQ5: the "AI area" bundles robotics, automation, big data and AR/VR, so the 4.8% is not comparable to Eurostat/ISTAT narrow AI use. Outcome is eco-innovation, not productivity.

authors: Cirillo, Valeria; Fanti, Lucrezia; Mina, Andrea; Ricci, Andrea
title: New digital technologies and firm performance in the Italian economy
population: Italian partnership and limited liability firms in the non-agricultural private sector with at least 5 employees, RIL-Orbis merged panel
ai_definition: Industry 4.0 dummy = 1 if the firm invested in at least one of IoT, robotics, big data analytics, augmented reality, cybersecurity in 2015-2017 (AI not measured separately).
coi_note: Academic and INAPP authors; no commercial interest.
notes: Version of record PDF (T&F layout) from Sant'Anna IRIS repository; PDF page = journal page minus 157. Data: INAPP-RIL 2018 (V wave) merged with Orbis, panel ~3,000 firms (regression N about 6,963-7,244 obs). Diff-in-Diff with firm FE, parallel-trend check (I4.0*2014 not significant) and PSM common support: quasi-causal. Definition includes cybersecurity, so I4.0 adoption rates (~37%) are much higher than AI-specific rates. Table A1 shows higher I4.0 incidence among larger firms (75.5% for 250+ employees), North vs South (25.8%). North-East figure 41.7% from same table. Effects concentrated in mature firms and SMEs; industry subsample effect 0.047* vs services n.s. AI not measured.

authors: Bettiol, Marco; Capestro, Mauro; Di Maria, Eleonora; Ganau, Roberto
title: Is this time different? How Industry 4.0 affects firms’ labor productivity
population: Manufacturing micro, small and medium enterprises in "Made in Italy" industries in six Northern Italian regions (Aida population of 7,714 firms)
geography: Northern Italy (Piedmont, Lombardy, Veneto, Trentino-South Tyrol, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Emilia Romagna)
ai_definition: First-time adoption (2010-2017) of at least one of seven Industry 4.0 technologies: advanced robotics, additive manufacturing, laser cutting, big data and cloud, 3D scanner, augmented reality, IoT and smart products (AI not measured separately).
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova, Pavia, LSE); no commercial interest.
notes: Version of record (CC BY) from LSE Research Online; PDF page = journal page minus 1447. Original CAWI survey (1,229 respondents, 15.9% response) merged with Aida balance sheets; 907 firms after cleaning, 6,460 firm-years. Two-way FE DiD with event study (no pre-trends), PSM and placebo tests: authors claim causal identification, but only 79 adopters and effect fades after 2 years. Coverage limited to Made in Italy industries in the North. Table 2 difficulties values mapped row-by-row from PDF text extraction (single percentage column; 7 rows: 87.30, 87.30, 85.71, 87.30, 88.89, 87.30, 84.13). Same survey family as bettiol2021districts (Padova 2017 survey), overlapping data. AI not measured.

org: Competitiveness Review: An International Business Journal

title: Industrial districts and the fourth industrial revolution
population: Manufacturing firms in 12 Made in Italy industries in Northern Italy (Aida population 8,002 firms, revenue > 1m EUR with exceptions)
geography: Northern Italy (Emilia Romagna, Friuli Venezia Giulia, Veneto, Trentino Alto Adige, Lombardia, Piemonte)

coi_note: Academic authors (Univ. Padova), funded by a university grant (BIRD161248/16); no commercial interest.
notes: Version of record (CC BY, Competitiveness Review 31(1):12-26); PDF page = journal page minus 11. Descriptive comparison of 20 district vs 20 matched non-district adopters (chi2/t-tests) plus one case study (Del Brenta, Riviera del Brenta footwear district): very small n, self-selection acknowledged. Results/effects are self-reported. District membership via ISTAT district classification. Non-district adoption rate implied 181/1,079 (16.8%, own computation, not stated). authors: Cefis, Elena; Scrofani, Stefania; Tubiana, Matteo
title: Innovation policies and firms' productivity: the Italian Industry 4.0 Plan for digital transformation
population: Population of Italian firms filing financial statements in AIDA (Bureau van Dijk) 2011-2019, excluding firms with median employment below one and ATECO sections O, P, R: 395,394 firms; 71,904 firms identified as users of at least one Industry 4.0 Plan incentive in 2018, 57,429 treated units retained after 1-nearest-neighbour PSM; DiD estimation sample 116,010 firms (932,598 firm-year observations)
fieldwork_period: Financial statements 2011-2019; treatment identified on 2016-2017 changes; post-treatment years 2018-2019
ai_definition: No AI measure. Treatment = inferred use of at least one Industry 4.0 Plan fiscal incentive (hyper and super depreciation, credit on innovation / Nuova Sabatini, R&D tax credit, patent box), detected from joint changes in balance-sheet and profit-and-loss items between 2016 and 2017 (for hyper depreciation: increase in tangible fixed assets and depreciation, with a more than proportional rise in the depreciation rate). AI listed among the nine Industry 4.0 pillars in the framing only.
coi_note: Academic authors (Bergamo, Sant'Anna Pisa, Politecnico di Torino); funding from University of Bergamo and, for one author, PagoPA S.p.A. and Sant'Anna; no commercial interest in the evaluated policy.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). The paper evaluates the Italian Industry 4.0 Plan on labour productivity using AIDA financial statements 2011-2019 for the population of Italian firms (395,394 after exclusions); beneficiaries are inferred from joint movements of balance-sheet items (71,904 treated in 2018, 19.4% of the pre-PSM sample, of which 12.85% via hyper/super depreciation), then 1-NN PSM plus firm fixed-effects DiD on 116,010 firms. Headline: +3.9% labour productivity (coefficient 0.0398, p<0.01), driven by hyper/super depreciation (0.0497) and Nuova Sabatini credit (0.0485); R&D tax credit and patent box have no short-run effect; micro (0.049) and large firms (0.050) gain most; low-tech manufacturing (0.0345) gains more than high-tech manufacturing (0.0254). AI is not measured separately: the treatment is the whole fiscal bundle and the technology adopted is unobserved (only inferred investment). Limitations: indirect treatment identification (possible false positives/negatives, partly addressed by peak-detection and investing-firm control robustness checks), only two post-treatment years, selection into treatment by larger and more productive firms. Relevance: RQ1 (take-up share of Industry 4.0 incentives by incentive and the under-representation of micro firms), RQ3 (financial constraints as the binding barrier, horizontal incentives as enabler only for firms already ready), RQ4 (quasi-causal productivity effect with size and sector heterogeneity), RQ5 (financial-statement based measurement as an alternative to survey data).

authors: Serafini, Luca; Marrocu, Emanuela; Paci, Raffaele
title: Smart strategies, smarter performance: the impact of S3 and industry 4.0 on firms’ outcomes
population: Italian private firms with a single ERDF-funded project in the 2014-2020 programming period, matched to ORBIS (all sectors: Industry NACE A-F, KIS, LKIS, Tourism)
fieldwork_period: ERDF 2014-2020 programming period; firm data from 2012 (OpenCoesione + ORBIS)
ai_definition: Industry 4.0 project = S3 category "Smart Factory" etc. or text analysis of project descriptions with EPO Fourth Industrial Revolution keywords; S3I4 = I4 project aligned with regional Smart Specialisation Strategy. Firm-level I4 investment, not AI specifically.
coi_note: Academic authors (Univ. Cagliari, CRENoS); open access; no commercial interest.
notes: Version of record (ICC 34(5):927-956, CC BY) from IRIS UniCa; PDF page = journal page minus 926. Data: OpenCoesione ERDF projects merged with ORBIS; 22,086 one-project firms, estimation sample 14,631 (0% vs 100% payment ratio). Callaway-Sant'Anna staggered DiD with not-yet-treated controls (all firms awarded funds): quasi-causal; parallel trends slightly violated at t-1 in one subsample (Rambachan-Roth sensitivity). Effects concentrated in North and Industry; Centre/South not significant. 92.8% of sample firms have 1-50 employees. Measures I4 funded projects, not AI; examples in text mention AI projects in services. Relevant for RQ3 (policy, North-South) and RQ4.

authors: Cucculelli, M.; Dileo, I.; Pini, M.
title: Filling the void of family leadership: institutional support to business model changes in the Italian Industry 4.0 experience
population: Italian manufacturing firms (NACE Rev.2 section C, 24 divisions) with at least 5 employees; stratified by industry, size class (5-9, 10-19, 20-49, 50+) and macro-area (North-West, North-East, Center, South)
ai_definition: No AI measure. Dependent variable is adoption of an Industry 4.0 business model: any activity targeted at value creation, value offer or value capture through digital technology (digitisation of processes, customer-tailored products, supplier/customer interaction), coded 0 = no 4.0 business model, 1 = planning, 2 = already adopted.
coi_note: Co-author M. Pini is at Centro Studi Tagliacarne (chambers of commerce research centre), linked to the Unioncamere data provider; no commercial interest. Open access (CC BY), funded by Univ. Politecnica delle Marche.
notes: Version of record read (Springer OA PDF). PDF page numbers given, journal pages 213-241 (PDF p.N = journal p.212+N). Data: Unioncamere/Tagliacarne 2019 CATI survey. Multinomial probit, cross-sectional, correlational (authors state the cross-sectional approach limits causality, PDF p.20). Estimation samples 603 (ownership models) and 2468 (management models). Adoption measure is 4.0 business models, not AI; only 3.2% had adopted, relevant for low I4.0 depth among Italian manufacturing SMEs and for family leadership as barrier and Triple Helix as enabler. Quotes of Table 2 and Table 4 are row reconstructions from the table layout.

authors: Neirotti, P.; Ricci, A.; Tubiana, M.
title: Industry 4.0 digital technologies and international performance: The role of family management in Italian firms
population: Italian partnerships and limited liability firms (private sector, all sectors) with at least 5 employees, longitudinal component of RIL-INAPP survey
fieldwork_period: RIL waves 2010, 2015, 2018; I4.0 adoption refers to 2015-2017
ai_definition: I4.0 digital technologies from RIL 2018 question 'In the period 2015-2017, did the firm invest in new technologies?' with options IoT, robotics, big data analytics, augmented reality; dummy = invested in at least one; split into information I4.0 DTs (IoT, big data analytics, augmented reality) and production I4.0 DTs (robotics). No separate AI item.
coi_note: Co-author A. Ricci is at INAPP, producer of the RIL survey used; no commercial interest.
notes: Version of record (article in press layout, 'xxx' pagination) read from the Politecnico di Torino IRIS copy; PDF p.1 is the IRIS cover, so PDF p.N = article p.N-1. Earlier WP version exists: INAPP WP n.116 (Feb 2024), 'Foreign markets and the nature of digital technologies' (not used). Data: RIL-INAPP (SISTAN) merged with ORBIS; about 3000 firms, 8562 pooled observations. Identification: PSM-matched difference-in-differences and triple DiD with firm FE and pre-trend test (quasi-causal, conditional on common trends); plus 5 qualitative case studies. Sample covers all private sectors, estimates include 2-digit sector FE but no manufacturing-only estimate in the published version. Relevant to RQ3 (family management as moderator/barrier) and RQ4 (effects on international performance). The significance legend in the tables reads '* at 1 %' (probably a typo for 10%).

authors: Cugno, M.; Castagnoli, R.; Büchi, G.
title: Openness to Industry 4.0 and performance: The impact of barriers and incentives
population: Local manufacturing units in Piedmont with at least two employees that adopted one or more I4.0 technologies (from Unioncamere Piemonte 'Congiuntura Industriale in Piemonte' survey of 1732 units); plus 9 expert interviews and multiple case studies
ai_definition: No AI item. Openness to Industry 4.0 = number of the 10 I4.0 pillars adopted (advanced manufacturing, augmented reality, IoT, big data, cloud, cyber security, additive manufacturing, simulation, horizontal/vertical integration, others); barriers (12 items grouped in knowledge, economic-financial, cultural, system) and incentives (Impresa 4.0 measures such as super- and hyper-amortisation, tax credits) counted as sums of dummies.
coi_note: No funding or commercial interest declared.
notes: Version of record read (University of Turin IRIS copy of the Elsevier PDF). Mixed methods: literature review, 9 expert interviews, multiple case studies, then parallel-serial mediation (OLS path analysis) on 500 adopting local units from the Unioncamere Piemonte survey. Cross-sectional, perceived performance (count of perceived opportunities), selection on adopters only: correlational despite 'causal' wording. Some inconsistencies in reported significance (e.g. H3a described as not significant yet accepted, p<0.1 thresholds for large t values). Useful for RQ3 (cultural and financial barriers, low information on incentives among SMEs, most-used incentives are tax-related amortisation) and regional data point for Piedmont.

authors: Büchi, G.; Cugno, M.; Castagnoli, R.
title: Smart factory performance and Industry 4.0
population: Local manufacturing units in Piedmont with at least two employees (Unioncamere Piemonte, Congiuntura Industriale in Piemonte); regressions on the 231 I4.0-adopting units
ai_definition: No AI item. I4.0 adoption = application of at least one of 10 pillars of enabling technologies (advanced manufacturing, augmented reality, IoT, big data, cloud, cyber security, additive manufacturing, simulation, horizontal/vertical integration, others). Breadth = number of pillars; depth = pillars used frequently along value-chain stages.
coi_note: No funding; authors declare no competing interest.
