Strong size gradient in I4.0 adoption relevant to RQ1/RQ3. Size class shares in the Table 3 quote are reconstructed from the table layout.

authors: Dottori, D.
title: Robots and employment: evidence from Italy
population: 784 Italian local labour markets (1991 definition), 1991-2016; incumbent manufacturing workers (INPS matched employer-employee sample, aged 22-41 in 1993, >=2 years tenure); entrant workers
ai_definition: No AI. Industrial robots (IFR, ISO 8373 definition) stock per 1000 workers by industry; local exposure = industry robot growth weighted by initial local employment shares; instrumented with robot growth in other European countries.
coi_note: Author at Bank of Italy; views are the author's own; no commercial interest.
notes: Version read: Bank of Italy Questioni di Economia e Finanza (Occasional Papers) n.572, July 2020 (DOI 10.32057/0.QEF.2020.572), not the Economia Politica version of record (38(2):739-795, paywalled, not opened); pages are QEF PDF pages (printed QEF page in brackets); figures in the journal version may differ. Data: IFR robots, Istat census/ASIA employment, INPS worker histories, OECD trade, EU KLEMS ICT. Causal IV design (shift-share with European instruments), long differences. About robots, not AI, and at local labour market/worker level rather than firm adoption: useful only as RQ4 benchmark on automation and employment in Italy (no harmful net employment effect).

org: International Journal of Operations & Production Management
authors: Leoni, L.; Ardolino, M.; El Baz, J.; Gueli, G.; Bacchetti, A.
title: The mediating role of knowledge management processes in the effective use of artificial intelligence in manufacturing firms
population: Senior executives of Italian manufacturing firms (random selection of 1,096 firms invited; respondents mainly machinery and equipment 40.8% and metal products 21.7%; skewed to larger firms, 26% with more than 1,000 employees)
fieldwork_period: Not stated in the paper (web survey; manuscript received 7 May 2022, so fieldwork before spring 2022)
ai_definition: Self-reported level of adoption of nine specific AI tools (machine learning, neural network, deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, cognitive computing, predictive analytics, robotic process automation, semantic search), each on a 5-point Likert scale; implementation and use of specific AI tools used as proxy of the AI adoption level. After measurement purification only ML, deep learning, computer vision and predictive analytics items are retained.
coi_note: Academic authors (Tor Vergata, Brescia, Ibn Zohr) plus one practitioner co-author (knowledge manager at MyData-TRUST); open access CC BY; no funding conflict stated.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Web survey of senior executives in 120 Italian manufacturing firms (11% response from 1,096 randomly selected firms; fieldwork date not stated), PLS-SEM (ADANCO) testing AI -> knowledge management processes -> supply chain resilience / firm performance. AI is measured on its own, not as part of an Industry 4.0 bundle: nine named AI tools (ML, neural networks, deep learning, computer vision, NLP, cognitive computing, predictive analytics, RPA, semantic search) rated on Likert scales, with item means below 1 on the retained items, indicating very low adoption even in a large-firm-skewed sample. Limitations: single informant, cross-sectional, self-reported perceptual performance, non-probabilistic response, sample skewed to large firms (26% above 1,000 employees; authors concede results are likely more positive than the national situation); the employee-size table sums to 127 rather than 120 and percentages are computed on 127, an unresolved inconsistency in the paper; significance labels in Table 8 (*** = p<0.01) differ from the earlier abstract-based coding (p<0.001), corrected here. Relevance: RQ2 (which AI tool families are surveyed in Italian manufacturing), RQ3 (knowledge management processes as the organisational enabler through which AI pays off; size positive), RQ4 (no direct AI effect on performance, beta 0.006 n.s.; indirect effect via KMPs 0.29; self-reported, correlational), RQ5 (tool-list operationalisation vs official statistics).

authors: Forgione, A.F.; Migliardo, C.
title: Disrupting regional efficiency gaps via Industry 4.0 firm investments
population: Italian manufacturing firms with 20 or more employees surveyed by the Bank of Italy Survey of Industrial and Service Firms (Invind), accessed through the Bank of Italy Remote Dataset (BIRD); stratified sample by sector, size and area; unbalanced panel 2016-2019 (6,274 firm-year observations)
geography: Italy, four macro-regions (Northwest, Northeast, Centre, South)
ai_definition: No separate AI measure. Variable Tech = share of Industry 4.0 investment in total firm investment expenditure, five classes (0%; 0.1-5%; 5.1-20%; 20.1-40%; >40.1%), following the National Industry 4.0 plan classification of advanced digital technologies (artificial intelligence and big data, IoT, industrial robotics, 3D printing).
coi_note: None identified; academic authors (University of Messina), no funding or sponsor disclosed in the text.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). One-step true random effects stochastic frontier analysis (translog, Mundlak correction) on Bank of Italy Invind microdata (BIRD) for about 2,600 Italian manufacturing firms with at least 20 employees, 2016-2019, relating technical inefficiency to the share of Industry 4.0 investment in total investment (five classes) and to macro-regional dummies. AI is not measured separately: artificial intelligence and big data are listed among the technologies in the Industry 4.0 investment bundle defined by the National Industry 4.0 plan, so the paper gives no AI-specific adoption rate. Descriptive tables give regional I4.0 investment rates (43.88% of observations with zero I4.0 investment overall, 58.12% in the South, 35.60% in the Northwest), and the SFA shows that I4.0 shares above 5% cut inefficiency by about 24% (49% above 40%), with the largest gains for Southern firms and no significant gains in Northeast and Centre. Limitations: correlational short panel, only macro-regional location, intensity (share) not level of investment, micro firms excluded; slight inconsistency between 2608 firms (p.6) and 2609 groups (abstract, Table 8 note). Relevant to RQ1 (North-South adoption gap in the I4.0 bundle, size classes), RQ3 (regional divide, policy incentives), RQ4 (efficiency and value-added effects, not causal) and RQ5 (investment-share operationalisation versus adoption dummies).

org: MEF Dipartimento delle Finanze, DF Working Papers (also SSRN)
authors: Bratta, B.; Romano, L.; Acciari, P.; Mazzolari, F.
title: The Impact of Digitalization Policies. Evidence from Italy’s Hyper-depreciation of Industry 4.0 Investments
population: Universe of Italian companies filing 2018 corporate tax returns (tax year 2017) merged with 2016 balance sheets and ANPAL job flows (about 381 thousand firms, 6,553 hyper-depreciation users); ISTAT ICT survey subsample of about 16 thousand firms with >=10 employees
fieldwork_period: Tax year 2017; job flows Jan 2016 - March 2019
ai_definition: No AI item. I4.0 investment = use of the 2017 hyper-depreciation allowance (iper-ammortamento, +150% tax base for 'smart' high-tech machinery and equipment controlled by computerised systems and ICT appliances), from corporate tax returns; ex-ante digital maturity classes from ISTAT ICT survey.
coi_note: Authors from the Ministry of Economy and Finance (which administers the incentive) and Centro Studi Confindustria (industry association that advocated Industria 4.0 incentives); policy-evaluation interest, not commercial.
notes: Read the DF Working Paper n.6/2020 (June 2020) PDF from finanze.gov.it (PDF page, printed WP page in brackets); SSRN 3648046 is the same paper (not peer reviewed as such). Crossref lists first author as 'bratta, barbara' (lowercase), capitalised here. Data: MEF corporate tax returns, Bureau van Dijk balance sheets, F24 forms, ISTAT ICT survey 2018, ANPAL job flows, UCIMU orders. Take-up and beneficiary characteristics descriptive; employment effect via PSM before-after (conditional independence, no quasi-experiment because the incentive was universal; authors admit omitted-variable bias cannot be ruled out). Hyper-depreciation covers smart machinery, not AI specifically. Additionality of the 7 bn euros not identified (p.12).

authors: Antonazzo, L.; Sansone, G.; Orel, M.
title: The Impact of Industry 4.0 and State Incentives on Firms' Skills Needs: An Empirical Investigation of the Italian Manufacturing Sector
population: Italian manufacturing firms (NACE C) that adopted Industry 4.0 technologies, purposively sampled from 114 candidates: 26 companies, 29 interviewees (one key informant per firm as a rule); counted from Table 1: 21 large, 2 medium, 3 small firms; 22 in the North (Piedmont 8, Lombardy 7, Emilia-Romagna 4, Friuli Venezia Giulia 2, Veneto 1), 2 in the Centre (Lazio, Marche), 2 in Apulia; sectors mainly motor vehicles (C29), machinery (C28), transport equipment (C30), rubber and plastics (C22)
fieldwork_period: Semi-structured remote interviews July to September 2022; follow-up email consultation with 13 of the 26 firms in August 2024
ai_definition: No AI-specific measure. Firms selected as adopters of Industry 4.0 technologies (IoT, big data, cloud manufacturing, robotics, AI, additive manufacturing listed as key enabling technologies); state incentives = Piano Nazionale Industria 4.0 / Transizione 4.0 tax incentives, R&D tax credit, subsidised loans and training support, discussed qualitatively.
coi_note: Academic authors (Prague University of Economics and Business, University of Salento, University College Dublin); no specific funding; authors declare no conflicts of interest.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Qualitative multiple case study (Gioia-style coding of 22 first-order categories into 8 themes and 2 dimensions) of 26 Italian manufacturing firms adopting Industry 4.0 (29 interviewees, July-September 2022, follow-up with 13 firms in August 2024), framed in Skill-Biased Technological Change theory. Proposes a three-category skills framework (technical, social, strategic) and finds that Piano Industria 4.0 / Transizione 4.0 incentives mostly subsidised already-planned investments, financed upskilling in existing technological domains and rarely produced new skill sets. AI is not measured or analysed separately: firms are Industry 4.0 adopters in general and AI appears only in the list of enabling technologies. No quantitative results; the only numbers are the sample description and a secondary Industry 4.0 adoption figure cited from Cirillo et al. 2023 (40% of firms 2015-2017, 33% small vs 77% large). Limitations: 21 of 26 firms are large and 22 of 26 are Northern (counted from Table 1), one informant per firm, no AI focus, abstract-based coding was correct (number of firms, period and region now filled). Relevance: RQ3 only (skills shortage and skills mix as barrier/enabler; incentives as enabler with limited additionality and no effect on skill composition).

authors: Ricci, R.; Battaglia, D.; Neirotti, P.
title: External knowledge search, opportunity recognition and industry 4.0 adoption in SMEs
population: Innovative manufacturing SMEs (<250 employees, turnover <50 million euro) in Piedmont, medium and high-tech OECD sectors, with at least one patent, publicly funded R&D project or acceleration programme in the previous three years; population surveyed 1,851 firms (with the Piedmont Chambers of Commerce), 367 responses (19.8%), 174 manufacturing SMEs retained
ai_definition: No AI-specific measure. Adoption measured for eight MISE Industry 4.0 technologies (IoT, big data and advanced analytics, simulation, integration of information systems, augmented and virtual reality, cyber security, additive manufacturing, collaborative robotics) on a 1-5 assimilation scale (1 no potential, 3 pilot, 5 in use); IoT, big data analytics, simulation and systems integration form the Information and Digital Technologies (IDT) construct, which the authors interpret as covering IoT, AI and big data.
coi_note: Academic authors (Politecnico di Torino); survey run with the Piedmont Chambers of Commerce; MIUR departments of excellence funding acknowledged. No commercial interest.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). CIS-style survey run in 2018 with the Piedmont Chambers of Commerce on 1,851 innovative firms (19.8% response), reduced to 174 manufacturing SMEs; PLS-SEM (5,000 bootstraps) tests whether breadth and depth of external knowledge search affect Industry 4.0 adoption through the recognition of digital design, digital manufacturing and digital servitisation opportunities. AI is not measured as a separate item: adoption is rated on a 1-5 assimilation scale for eight MISE technologies, and the IDT construct (IoT, big data analytics, simulation, systems integration) is what the authors loosely call 'IoT, AI, Big Data'. Useful descriptive depth figures: mean assimilation 2.10 for IDT, 2.42 cyber security, 1.92 additive manufacturing, 1.73 cobots, 1.52 AR/VR, i.e. between 'known but no initiative' and 'pilot' even among innovative SMEs. Headline paths: breadth -> IDT total 0.172 (fully mediated, mostly via servitisation 0.386); depth -> digital design 0.281 and digital manufacturing 0.246; size, age and R&D intensity not significant. Limitations: opt-in sample of innovative firms in one region (not representative of Italian manufacturing), cross-sectional, self-reported single informant. Relevance: RQ3 (ecosystem collaboration, competence centres and DIHs as enablers), RQ1 (depth of adoption at pilot stage in 2018), RQ2 (functions: design, manufacturing, servitisation), RQ5 (assimilation-scale measurement versus binary adoption).

authors: Lepore, D.; Micozzi, A.; Spigarelli, F.
title: Industry 4.0 Accelerating Sustainable Manufacturing in the COVID-19 Era: Assessing the Readiness and Responsiveness of Italian Regions
population: Italian NUTS-2 regions (regional indicators from ISTAT firm samples, 2014 and 2016); secondary use of the MET-MISE survey of about 24,000 Italian companies (2017-2018) for I4.0 adoption by region; regional I4.0 support measures issued March to September 2020
fieldwork_period: Indicators 2014 and 2016 (ISTAT); MET-MISE survey 2017-2018; policy mapping Phase 1 (March-May 2020) and Phase 2 (May-September 2020)
ai_definition: No AI-specific measure. I4.0 adoption taken from MET-MISE (share of 'enterprises 4.0' vs traditional enterprises with or without 4.0 plans); readiness proxied by six regional indicators: firms with product/process innovation, innovation expenditure per worker, cooperation agreements for innovation, broadband, tertiary education, S&T employment.
coi_note: Academic authors (University of Macerata, University E-Campus); no commercial interest.
notes: Descriptive regional study: (1) readiness index from ISTAT regional indicators plus cluster analysis, (2) mapping of regional I4.0/remote-working support measures after COVID-19. No firm-level estimation, no AI measure, no manufacturing breakdown; I4.0 adoption figures are secondary (MET-MISE, 24,000 companies, 2017-2018) and the text says Piedmont 11.7% while Table 2 reports 11.8 (column order inferred from text: 3rd column = enterprises 4.0). Correlational only; north-south divide (readiest: Emilia-Romagna, Lombardy, Friuli, Piedmont, Veneto). Full text read from the author copy of the published version on the University of Macerata repository (u-pad.unimc.it), identical layout to MDPI version (19 pages); MDPI site blocked. Page numbers = article pages.

authors: Menicacci, L.
title: Real effects of investment tax incentives: evidence from Italian private firms
population: Private (unlisted) non-financial firms of the automotive and automation industries: 72 treated firms in South Tyrol (Italy) self-declared as Industry 4.0 firms (list from IDM Chamber of Commerce Bozen-Bolzano and NOI Tech Park) and 76 control firms in the Austrian Laender Kaernten, Tyrol and Vorarlberg in the same 4-digit NACE codes; 148 firms, 888 firm-year observations; 55% manufacturing (NACE C)
geography: Italy (South Tyrol / Alto Adige) vs Austria (Kaernten, Tyrol, Vorarlberg)
fieldwork_period: Financial statements 2014-2019 (pre-bonus 2014-2016, bonus era 2017-2019; 2013 and 2020 used for lags and leads), ORBIS data
ai_definition: No AI measure. Treatment is being an Italian (South Tyrol) firm self-declared as Industry 4.0, used as a proxy for use of Hyper-Depreciation (iperammortamento, +150% deductible cost on interconnected hi-tech machinery, +40% on related software), compared with Austrian firms with no equivalent scheme, over 2017-2019 vs 2014-2016 (DiD with entropy balancing).
coi_note: Single academic author (Free University of Bozen-Bolzano); no commercial interest identified; no funding statement seen.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Border-region difference-in-differences: 72 private South Tyrol firms in automotive and automation (self-declared Industry 4.0 firms, proxy for Hyper-Depreciation use; 55.6% manufacturing) vs 76 Austrian firms in Kaernten, Tyrol and Vorarlberg, ORBIS accounts 2014-2019, entropy balancing, classic and firm/year fixed-effects DiD. Treat x Hyper raises total fixed investment by 0.027 of lagged assets (p<0.01), tangible 0.019-0.023, intangible 0.006-0.007 (about 997 and 301 thousand euro per treated firm; 10.2% vs 33.2% of asset stock), has no effect on employment, raises operating income per employee (10.286, p<0.05, firm/year FE) and lowers the GAAP effective tax rate by 12.8 points. Prior abstract-based coding was correct in direction; the fieldwork period, sample size (148 firms, 888 firm-years) and the automotive/automation focus were unknown and are now recorded; manufacturing_coverage changed from none to sector_breakdown_incl_manufacturing because Table 1 reports NACE sections (C = 55%). AI is not measured: the treatment is the Industry 4.0 hyper-depreciation bundle and firm self-identification as Industry 4.0. Limitations: tiny, single-province, two-industry sample; treatment is self-declared Industry 4.0 status rather than observed incentive use; overlap with super-depreciation; pre-COVID window only; no size-class breakdown. Relevance: RQ3 (fiscal incentive as enabler and tax-planning lever) and RQ4 (quasi-causal investment and productivity effects without job losses), to be cited with caution given coverage.

org: Journal of Entrepreneurship, Management and Innovation (JEMI)
authors: Pini, M.
title: Family management and Industry 4.0: Different effects in different geographical areas? An analysis of the less developed regions in Italy
population: Italian manufacturing SMEs with 5-249 employees (Unioncamere survey), analysis restricted to family businesses (about 80% of sample)
ai_definition: Dummy = 1 if the firm invested in at least one of the nine topics of Italy's Industry 4.0 plan (advanced manufacturing solutions, additive manufacturing, augmented reality, simulation, horizontal/vertical integration, industrial Internet, cloud, cyber security, big data and analytics) during 2017 to mid-2018. coi_note: Author is Senior Economist at Unioncamere-Si.Camera, the body that ran the survey; views stated as personal; no commercial interest.
notes: Unioncamere (Chambers of Commerce) survey, early 2018, record-linked to administrative archive; probit with average marginal effects, cross-sectional and correlational (no causal identification). Key messages: I4.0 investment lower in the South; external management raises I4.0 adoption in the Centre-North, while in the South it matters only combined with R&D; human capital (graduates) positive in both areas; past innovators more likely to invest (innovation divide). Author warns Southern results less reliable (346 obs). Limitations: binary I4.0 variable (no intensity), no ownership concentration or balance-sheet controls. Full text (VoR, OA CC BY) read; PDF page numbers given with journal page in brackets.

authors: Segarra-Blasco, A.; Tomàs-Porres, J.; Teruel, M.
title: AI, robots and innovation in European SMEs
population: SMEs (1-250 employees, with a subsample of larger firms) in the Flash Eurobarometer 486; analysis focused on the EU-27
geography: EU-27 (Italy included in the 'Mediterranean' cluster with Spain, Portugal, Cyprus); survey also covers non-EU countries
ai_definition: Self-reported dummy: whether the firm has adopted 'AI and machine learning' among seven advanced digital technologies listed in Flash Eurobarometer 486 (AI/ML, cloud, robots, smart devices/sensors, big data analytics, high-speed infrastructure, blockchain).
coi_note: Academic authors (Universitat Rovira i Virgili); public research funding; authors declare no competing interests.
notes: Flash Eurobarometer 486 (TNS for the European Commission, GESIS ZA7637), cross-sectional; two-stage residual inclusion (bivariate probit for AI/robot adoption instrumented with country DESI indicators, then multivariate probit on product/process/organisational/marketing innovation). Authors state cross-sectional data prevent causal claims and the IV does not fully remove endogeneity. No Italy-specific estimate: Italy only enters through the Mediterranean cluster (Spain, Italy, Portugal, Cyprus; p.11 fn 13), whose AI share (7.52%) is below Northern/Core and above Eastern. Internal inconsistencies: p.8 says 6.9% AI and 8.3% robots (Table 6) while Table 8 gives 7.24%/9.12%; p.9 text reports blockchain and AI as 7.2% and 3.1% but Table 10 gives AI 7.24% and blockchain 3.11% (labels apparently swapped). Scale-ups and start-ups adopt more; size, exporting and country digital skills/infrastructure drive adoption; in manufacturing AI/robots serve more specialised innovation roles. Estimation n = 10,626. Full text (VoR, OA) read from URV repository copy; page numbers = PDF pages (journal pages 719-745).

authors: Kinkel, S.; Baumgartner, M.; Cherubini, E.
title: Prerequisites for the adoption of AI technologies in manufacturing – Evidence from a worldwide sample of manufacturing companies
population: Managers (production, supply chain, technology management) of manufacturing companies in 16 industrial nations incl. Italy (n=49, 7.5%); ~40% SMEs <250 employees, 36% firms >1000 employees
geography: Cross-national, 16 countries: Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, India, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Poland, Russia, South Korea, Spain, Sweden, United Kingdom, USA
ai_definition: Use of AI/ML for three purposes: (i) analysis of large amounts of data, (ii) support for planning and optimisation of business processes, (iii) autonomous decision-making; each scored 0 = no use, 1 = pilot, 2 = some areas, 3 = all areas; AI use index = mean of the three (0-3). Any non-zero score (incl. pilots) counts as use.
coi_note: Academic authors (Karlsruhe University of Applied Sciences, ILIN); no funding conflict stated in the text.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). International online survey (Sept-Oct 2019) of 655 production/supply-chain/technology managers in manufacturing firms from 16 countries, including 49 Italian firms (7.5%); OLS regressions of a 0-3 AI use index on TOE factors, plus a logit on exclusively domestic AI use (n=443 AI users). AI is measured on its own, separately from the Industry 4.0 bundle, via three AI/ML purposes (data analysis, planning/optimisation, autonomous decision-making), but any pilot counts as use, so the headline rates (62%, 59%, 54%) are far above official statistics and are not comparable with Istat/Eurostat definitions; the sample is non-probabilistic and skewed to large firms (36% above 1000 employees). Italy-specific results are limited to the country dummy (not significant) and a descriptive 'midfield' position on digital skills; Table 4 (AI index by country) is an image not captured in the text. Relevance: RQ3 (digital skills index is the strongest enabler, coefficient 0.48, adj. R2 from 0.19 to 0.31; size positive; R&D intensity absorbed by skills), RQ5 (self-reported exec survey with pilot-inclusive definition vs official statistics; warning that descriptive country rankings vanish in multivariate models), RQ1 only as an international benchmark with an Italian sub-sample too small for inference.

org: OECD Science, Technology and Industry Working Papers (No. 2023/02)

Weighted LPM/OLS with 2-digit sector FE; Italy regressions do not control for firm age (p.47). Correlational: authors conclude the AI productivity premium is largely driven by selection and complementary assets (Italy's coefficient loses significance, p.53). Italy's size gradient is monotonic (p.28); manufacturing shows relatively high AI shares in recent-data countries incl. Italy (p.34). Figure bar values for Italy are graphical only and not extracted. OECD working paper, not peer-reviewed journal article. Full text read (OECD PDF, 86 pages); page numbers = PDF pages (equal to printed pages).

authors: Cullen, Z.; Faia, E.; Guglielminetti, E.; Perez-Truglia, R.; Rondinelli, C.

fieldwork_period: INVIND 2025 wave (February-May 2025) with follow-up in 2026 wave
ai_definition: Self-reported current use (experimental/limited or extensive) and intended use by 2027 of predictive AI, generative AI and robotics in a dedicated INVIND module; earlier waves ask AI adoption in general.
coi_note: Two authors are Bank of Italy economists (survey owner); academic co-authors; no commercial interest.

No significant effect on AI adoption intentions (only robotics). Effect stronger among firms not using Transition 4.0 incentive (0.918 vs 0.420, difference not significant, p.34). Cross-source contrast useful for RQ5: footnote cites EU ICT survey 2025 at 8.2% AI for Italian firms (10+ employees) vs 13.5% EU, vs 28% in INVIND (20+ employees, broader question). NBER working paper (revised August 2026), NOT peer-reviewed. Page numbers = PDF pages (printed page = PDF page minus 2).

authors: Battaglia, D.; Galati, F.; Molinaro, M.; Pessot, E.
title: Full, hybrid and platform complementarity: Exploring the industry 4.0 technology-performance link
population: 13 Italian I4.0 experts (6 Competence Center directors/general managers, 3 national research center researchers, 3 Digital Innovation Hub representatives, 1 system-integrator CEO) plus 152 I4.0 use cases published by Italian Competence Centers
ai_definition: No adoption rate; AI treated as one of the I4.0 'data processing' technologies (with big data and analytics) whose stand-alone and bundled applications (e.g. IoT + AI, robot + AI) are coded from interviews and use cases.
coi_note: Academic authors; informants are Competence Centers promoting I4.0, whose published use cases are showcase material (possible positive-outcome bias).
notes: Qualitative multi-source study (systems theory lens): expert interviews triangulated with Competence Center use cases, websites, reports and a white paper; only manufacturing cases retained. Identifies full, hybrid and platform complementarities; bundles have broader performance effects than single technologies. No adoption rates, no causal identification; performance numbers are self-reported by use cases. Authors flag Italian and Competence-Center perspective limits generalisability and call for data to test causal effects. Full text (VoR, OA CC BY-NC-ND) read from University of Siena IRIS copy; page numbers = PDF pages.

org: Economics of Innovation and New Technology (Taylor & Francis)

ai_definition: No AI measure. microDESI composite of four equally weighted dimensions: ICT training (specialist and generic), broadband >=100 Mbps, fractional count of digital technologies adopted (3D printing, cloud, big data in both years; applications, e-commerce, AR, cybersecurity in 2018; IoT and robots in 2020), share of e-government services used.
coi_note: Academic authors (Roma Tre) and Ministry of Economy and Finance (Treasury) economists; views not official; no commercial interest.

Full text read from Roma Tre IRIS copy of the published OA version (with T&F cover page): PDF page = printed page + 1.

authors: Corò, G.; Plechero, M.; Rullani, F.; Volpe, M.

fieldwork_period: Unioncamere Veneto survey collected in 2019; adoption years and workforce panel 2008-2018
ai_definition: Firm-reported adoption (and year of introduction) of 9 Industry 4.0 enabling technologies: Artificial Intelligence, Automation and Robotics, Additive Manufacturing, IoT, Virtual and Augmented Reality, Cloud Services, Cyber Security, Big Data Analytics, Blockchain; adoption modelled as a dummy marking the year of adoption
coi_note: Academic; data from Unioncamere Veneto, Veneto Lavoro and Osservatorio Economico-Sociale Treviso; EU H2020 MAKERS funding; WP states no conflict of interest
notes: Version read: Ca' Foscari Dept. of Economics Working Paper No. 12/WP/2020, 'The Evolution of Technological Space and Firms' Workforce Composition in a Manufacturing Region' (same authors, 35 pp.), the precursor of the Regional Studies article; the version of record (T&F) and the IRIS Ca' Foscari copy (closed access) and figshare file (only supplementary material, WAF-blocked) could not be opened. authors: Venturini, F.
title: Intelligent technologies and productivity spillovers: Evidence from the Fourth Industrial Revolution
population: 32 industrialized economies (country-level panel), incl. Italy and 18 EU member states (GB included)
geography: 32 countries (OECD, EU, China, Singapore); Italy included

coi_note: none (academic, University of Perugia and NIESR)

org: ECB Occasional Paper Series (No 395); also posted on SSRN

org: Journal of the International Council for Small Business
authors: Calabrese, G. G.; Falavigna, G.; Ippoliti, R.
title: Industry 4.0 and innovation policy: An investigation of SMEs in the Italian automotive supply chain
population: SMEs of the Italian automotive supply chain responding to the national survey of the Observatory on the Italian Automotive Supply Chain (Chamber of Commerce of Turin, ANFIA, CAMI Ca' Foscari; frame of more than 2,000 firms per year, response rate 25%), merged with AIDA, Ceris Rating and Ministry of Justice data; main analysis 151 SMEs in 2019, pooled 2019-2020 samples of 328-356 observations

Ordered logit, probit/IV probit and OLS on the Observatory on the Italian Automotive Supply Chain survey (25% response from a frame of 2,000+ firms; 151 SMEs in 2019, 328-356 pooled 2019-2020 observations) merged with AIDA, Ceris Rating and judicial-delay data. authors: Cirillo, V.; Mina, A.; Ricci, A.
title: Digital technologies, labor market flows and training: Evidence from Italian employer-employee data

coi_note: Academic (Univ. Bari, Sant'Anna Pisa) and RFF-CMCC/INAPP authors; PRIN funding.
notes: Version read: LEM Working Paper 2024/22 (September 2024, DOI 10.57838/sssa/qm5v-4c08), same title and authors as the TFSC article (vol. 209, 123735, December 2024), which is open access but whose publisher page was not retrievable (ScienceDirect 403 for both curl and WebFetch). Pages are PDF pages of the WP (printed page = PDF page minus 1). Figures of the journal version may differ marginally. Method: diff-in-diff with firm fixed effects and PSM robustness; common-trend test passed for hiring and separations. Documents the composition of the 2015-2017 Italian 'Industry 4.0' bundle: mostly cybersecurity, with IoT and robotics marginal (RQ5), and a positive net employment effect with no significant skill upgrading except for robotics (RQ4).

Digital technologies in general, not AI alone; Italy appears only as a country dummy with higher self-assessed adoption than France, which contrasts with Eurostat AI rankings (RQ5: self-assessed 'advanced technologies' is not AI use). Same Eurobarometer wave as ardito2025airevenue (11,429 obs after cleaning).

authors: Cattaruzzo, S.; Coro, G.; Borsato, R.
title: Technological complexity and global capabilities in SMEs. A survey in an Italian industrial region

ai_definition: Technological Complexity Index (Hidalgo-Hausmann economic complexity algorithm) over 14 technologies scored 1 = adopted, 0.5 = planned, 0 = not adopted; artificial intelligence is one of the 14 items (complexity value 3.730), alongside cloud, cybersecurity, robotics, IoT, big data, additive manufacturing, digital twin, AR/VR, blockchain, metaverse, nanotech, RFID, data integration
coi_note: Academic authors (Ca' Foscari Venice); Unioncamere Veneto survey.

Pages are PDF pages of the WP. Figures may differ in the published version. The AI adoption share itself is not reported (only the complexity ranking, where AI is among the least ubiquitous technologies, and the mean of 2.1 technologies per firm). Correlational Heckman estimates; representativeness of the 2,000-firm survey not detailed in the WP.

authors: Agostino, M.; Brancati, E.; Giunta, A.; Scalera, D.; Trivieri, F.
title: Digital technologies and global value chains: evidence from the Italian industry
population: Italian industrial firms (manufacturing, all size classes including micro 1-9 employees) in the MET survey, 2017 and 2019 waves (about 25,000 cross-sectional observations per wave, stratified by size, NUTS-2 region and industry); DT item available for 16,946 observations, benchmark Probit on 11,605; balance sheets from BvD-AIDA
geography: Italy (regional fixed effects, no regional breakdown reported)
fieldwork_period: MET waves 2017 and 2019 (each reporting data for the previous year); new adoption 2017-2019
ai_definition: No AI measure: DT = use or planned use of at least one of eleven MET technologies (collaborative robots, 3D printers, augmented reality, simulations/virtual tests, nanotechnologies and intelligent materials, electronic integration of data in production, electronic information sharing with customers/suppliers, industrial IoT, cloud, big data analytics, cyber-security), split into operational (OPDT) and informational (INFDT). The authors state that AI is not covered and could be added in future research.
coi_note: Academic authors (Calabria, Sapienza, Roma Tre, Sannio); no conflict of interest reported (p. 24).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Probit/Poisson, Lewbel and external IV, PSM and Oster bounds on MET survey microdata for Italian industrial firms (2017 and 2019 waves, about 25,000 observations each, micro firms included; DT item for 16,946 observations, benchmark regressions on 11,605), relating lagged GVC participation and governance mode to adoption of eleven Industry 4.0 technologies. AI is NOT among the MET items and the authors list its inclusion as future work, so the paper measures the Industry 4.0 bundle only; the earlier abstract-based ai_definition was incomplete on this point. Italy-specific manufacturing figures: DT adoption (use or planned) 19% micro, 33% small, 50% medium, 66% large; operational DT 14/22/39/58%; GVC participation raises adoption probability by about 4 pp (6-7 pp under relational governance), with the largest relative gain for micro firms (multiplier 1.27 vs 1.08 for large). Limitations: planned use counted as adoption in the benchmark, correlational design acknowledged, no regional or sectoral breakdown shown. Relevance: RQ1 (size gradient in Industry 4.0 adoption among Italian manufacturers, including micro firms rarely covered by Istat), RQ3 (GVC participation and relational buyer-supplier governance as enablers; debt, managerial and liquidity constraints as barriers), RQ5 (MET survey as a source family with planned-use items).

authors: Cucculelli, M.; Lamperti, F.; Mondolo, J.; Pompei, F.; Venturini, F.
title: Firm adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies in times of economic turmoil: the role of enabling factors
population: Italian firms with fewer than 1,000 employees, all sectors (agriculture, manufacturing, services); frame of about 369,000 firms from AIDA-BvD, random 15% stratified by industry, size and region (about 60,000 units); wave 1 (2019-2020) 16,492 respondents, 4,214 usable after matching with balance sheets; wave 2 (2022) about 1,000 answers, balanced panel of 794 firms (1,588 firm-year observations)
geography: Italy (national; fixed effects for 20 NUTS-2 regions, robustness with NUTS-3 provinces)
fieldwork_period: Wave 1: October 2019 to February 2020 (pre-Covid); wave 2: 20 September to December 2022 (post emergency status); skills and incentives referred to 2015-2019 and 2020-2022
ai_definition: No AI item. Outcome I40_Tech = 1 if at least one I4.0 technology (IoT, big data analytics, interconnected production cells, industrial robots, additive manufacturing, augmented reality, wearables) is 'under development/ongoing' at survey time; enabling technologies (management software incl. ERP, MES, SCADA, PLM, SCM, BI, CRM; cloud computing; cybersecurity) counted only if already in use; new technological skills = hiring digital specialists or targeted training (TechSk dummy). Three-stage adoption question per technology: in use / under development / not adopted.
coi_note: Academic authors (Universita Politecnica delle Marche, Universita Cattolica Milano, Perugia, Urbino); authors declare no competing interests; data available on request.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Two-wave own survey of Italian firms with fewer than 1,000 employees (frame about 369,000 AIDA firms, 15% stratified random sample; wave 1 Oct 2019-Feb 2020, 16,492 respondents, 27.5% response, 4,214 usable; wave 2 Sept-Dec 2022, 24% response, balanced panel 794 firms) matched with AIDA balance sheets and the National State Aid Register; probit (cross-sections, panel RE, pooled) with average marginal effects, Greene (2010) interaction effects, eprobit endogeneity checks and Poisson count models. 'Economic turmoil' = the Covid-19 pandemic (2020-2021), modelled as a symmetric shock between the two waves. AI is NOT a surveyed item: the outcome is ongoing adoption of any of seven I4.0 technologies (IoT, big data analytics, interconnected cells, industrial robots, additive manufacturing, AR, wearables) and the regressors are enabling technologies already in use (management software, cloud, cybersecurity) and new technological skills (hiring or targeted training). Key figures: new I4.0 adoption 29.47% (2019) and 30.35% (2022), 29.91% pooled, consistent with 26% in RIL 2015-2017; enabling tech 72.92% to 83.5%; firms investing in digital skills fell from 41.6% to 28.8%; by size, new I4.0 adoption 23.93% micro, 32.35% very small, 35.25% small, 43.51% medium, 28.57% large (n=14). Effects: skills AME 0.071 (2019) and 0.147 (2022), enabling tech alone not significant, I4.0 incentives +0.11 to +0.14, family firms -0.11 to -0.13; complementarity (both factors vs neither) +8.1 p.p. in 2019 and +22.5 p.p. in 2022, panel +17.4 p.p.; intensive margin 16-37 p.p. more technologies. Limitations: binary measures, sample over-represents structured manufacturing and business services, very few large firms, Covid-specific shock, ongoing-adoption outcome (not stock of adopters), online appendix tables (A4-A13) not in the PDF. Relevance: RQ3 (skills as the binding enabler, complementarity with precursor technologies, role of Industria 4.0 incentives, family ownership as a brake), RQ1 (Italy-wide I4.0 adoption rates by size and sector 2019-2022, no AI figure), RQ5 (ongoing vs completed adoption as a measurement choice; triangulation with RIL-INAPP).

authors: Buarque, B.; Casas, P.; Fernandez-Macias, E.; Gonzalez-Vazquez, I.; Hynes, R.; Kogler, D. F.; Salotti, S.
title: The geography of artificial intelligence in European regions: innovation, exposure and use
population: EU NUTS-2 regions (230 regions for patents); six regional indicators: EPO AI patents 1980-2019 and AI centrality index 2015-19, two occupational exposure shares computed on the 2023 Eurostat LFS, worker AI use from the JRC AIM-WORK survey (70,316 individuals, 2024-25) and firm AI adoption from Eurostat ICT usage in enterprises (isoc_r_eb_ain2, 2024 or 2023), the latter available for Italy only at national level
geography: EU27 NUTS-2 regions (Italy included; firm-level AI adoption for Italy at NUTS-0 only; Northern Italy named among patent concentrations)
fieldwork_period: Patents 1980-2019 (AICI 2015-19); exposure 2023 LFS; worker use 2024-2025; firm adoption 2023-2024; GDP 2023; education 2024; trade openness 2017
ai_definition: Six complementary indicators: AI patents (WIPO 2019 keywords plus CPC codes), AI centrality index, research-based (Tolan et al.) and expectation-based (Felten et al.) occupational exposure shares, worker self-reported use of an AI-powered tool at work in the last 12 months (AIM-WORK), and share of firms using AI from the Eurostat ICT usage in enterprises survey (isoc_r_eb_ain2, all activities)
coi_note: European Commission JRC and University College Dublin authors; no conflict of interest reported (p. 18); views not an official Commission position.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Policy Debates article mapping six regional AI indicators across EU NUTS-2 regions: EPO AI patents (27,154 families, 1980-2019) and an AI centrality index, two occupational exposure shares (2023 LFS), worker AI use from the JRC AIM-WORK survey (70,316 respondents, 2024-25) and firm AI adoption from the Eurostat ICT usage in enterprises survey (2023-24). AI is measured on its own (not inside an Industry 4.0 bundle) but at regional level, descriptively (population-weighted correlations only, no causal claims), and for all activities with no sector or size breakdown. Italy appears only as 'Northern Italy' among patent concentrations and in footnote 1, which states that Eurostat firm-level AI adoption for Italy is available at national level only, so no Italian regional adoption value exists in the paper. Limitations: survey self-reports, uneven territorial granularity, timing mismatches between indicators (openness 2017). Relevance: RQ1 (firm adoption concentrated, most regions below 15 per cent, vs widespread worker use around 30 per cent; firm adoption correlates 0.72 with GDP per capita), RQ3 (capability, skills and organisational frictions behind the implementation gap), RQ5 (worker-level vs firm-level measurement diverge; patents vs surveys). Useful as EU benchmark and for the breadth-vs-depth framing, not for Italian manufacturing figures.

authors: Grando, A.; Belvedere, V.; Chiarini, A.; D'Angelo, V.
title: The effect of industry 4.0 and lean management on operational performance improvement: evidence from Italy
population: Manufacturing plants located in Italy that implement both Lean Production and Industry 4.0, identified through AIDA plus industry associations, university thematic groups and LinkedIn (nearly 700 eligible companies); 189 usable questionnaires from shop-floor improvement managers (23.8 per cent under 50 employees, 37.6 per cent 50-249, 38.6 per cent over 250); plus interviews in seven plants
fieldwork_period: not stated; online survey in two waves, one-year observation window, before submission on 26 September 2024
ai_definition: Degree of adoption of Industry 4.0 measured by nine 5-point Likert items (Tortorella and Fettermann 2018, BCG list): IoT, cloud computing, cybersecurity, big data and analytics, simulation, horizontal and vertical integration, additive manufacturing, advanced manufacturing solutions, augmented reality; aggregated into a single TEC score and a high/low cluster. No AI item; AI and machine learning appear only in one interview case.
coi_note: Academic authors (Bocconi SDA, Cattolica, Verona, CNR ISSIRFA); no conflict declared; open access CC BY.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Mixed-method study: online survey of 189 Italian plants pre-selected as implementing both lean and Industry 4.0 (nearly 700 eligible, 27 per cent response, two waves, fieldwork undated but before September 2024; large plants over-represented at 38.6 per cent), cluster analysis, contingency tables and hierarchical regressions, plus seven interviews. AI is not isolated: I4.0 is a single 9-item Likert score (BCG list, with big data and analytics as one item); machine learning and AI appear only in the defence-company interview. The abstract-based coding was correct but incomplete; the key quantitative result is that I4.0 has no significant effect on overall self-rated performance in the full sample (beta 0.111) but positive effects on five attributes, and in plants with more than two years of lean the LP x TEC interaction is negative and significant (overall -2.296, productivity -1.522, quality -1.600). Limitations: adopters-only frame (no adoption rate for the population), self-assessed improvement over three years, cross-sectional, no fieldwork dates. Relevance: RQ2 (predictive maintenance and AGV use cases), RQ3 (barriers: worker resistance, top-down IT-led projects, non digitally native workforce, loss of shop-floor data ownership; enablers: leadership, training, early involvement), RQ4 (self-reported effects, contingent on lean maturity, no causal identification), RQ5 (I4.0 bundle scores versus technology-specific measures).

org: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
authors: Cimino, A.; Corvello, V.; Troise, C.; Thomas, A.; Tani, M.
title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption for Sustainable Growth in SMEs: An Extended Dynamic Capability Framework
population: Italian innovative startups listed in the Business Register of Innovative Startups, all sectors (58% services and utilities, 22% industry and manufacturing, 10% ICT); 81% with 10 or fewer employees
fieldwork_period: 15 November 2024 to 10 January 2025 (online questionnaire via email, LinkedIn, WhatsApp)
ai_definition: Two reflective constructs on 7-point Likert scales: AI Adoption Intensity (AIAI, 3 items: 'We have implemented AI in all our company processes', 'Relative to the potential of AI ... our AI implementation is extensive', 'AI has substantially changed our business processes', adapted from Chen and Tajdini 2024) and AI Acceptance Rate (AIAR, 2 items on readiness and willingness to adopt AI, adapted from Almaiah et al. 2022). No specific AI technology or use case is measured.
coi_note: Academic authors (Messina, Torino, Wroclaw, Napoli Federico II); open access via CRUI-CARE agreement; authors declare nothing to report.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Cross-sectional PLS-SEM (SEMinR, 5,000 bootstraps) on 210 Italian innovative startups surveyed 15 Nov 2024 to 10 Jan 2025 through email, LinkedIn and WhatsApp (non-probabilistic, response rate not reported); 81% have 10 or fewer employees and only 22% (45 firms) are in industry and manufacturing, with no manufacturing-specific estimates. AI is measured on its own (not an Industry 4.0 bundle) but only as two perceptual constructs, AI Adoption Intensity (3 items) and AI Acceptance Rate (2 items), without any named technology, use case or adoption rate, and all performance outcomes are self-reported Likert items. Minor internal inconsistencies between text and Table 7 (DC->TP 0.47 vs 0.447; AIAI->CP 0.288 vs 0.268; H12 reported as p=0.010 yet rejected on the confidence interval). Relevance: RQ3 (dynamic capabilities as enabler of AI readiness and adoption intensity), RQ4 (self-reported association between AI intensity and economic/technological performance, no effect on sustainability performance; non-causal), RQ5 (example of perceptual Likert operationalisation far from official adoption statistics); low weight for the manufacturing focus of the review.

authors: Benedetti, I.; Crescenzi, F.; Laureti, T.; Salvini, N.
title: Business digitalization in Italy: A comprehensive analysis using supplementary fuzzy set approach
population: Italian enterprises with at least 10 employees in industry and services (ISTAT ICT Usage and E-Commerce in Enterprises survey 2019; sample for 10-249 employees, census above 250); manufacturing (ATECO C) n=4,197
geography: Italy (NUTS 1 macro-areas: Northwest, Northeast, Centre, South, Islands)
ai_definition: AI is NOT measured: the fuzzy 'technological deprivation' index uses 47 ISTAT ICT survey items in seven dimensions (ERP/CRM software, computers and internet, website and data tracking, social media, cybersecurity, ICT skills and training, web sales); the survey section on AI technologies is mentioned but no AI, cloud or IoT variable enters the index. AI appears only in the discussion, citing the Istat Rapporto Annuale on larger firms combining AI, enterprise software and analytics.
coi_note: Academic authors (University of Tuscia); funded by Rome Technopole (PNRR, NextGenerationEU); competing-interest declaration limited to this funding.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Builds a fuzzy supplementary 'technological deprivation' index (Betti-Verma approach, alpha=2, jackknife variance) from 47 items of the 2019 ISTAT ICT survey microdata on 19,769 enterprises with at least 10 employees, reported by macro-sector, ATECO section, NUTS 1 area and size class. Correction to the abstract-based coding: AI is not measured, neither on its own nor within an Industry 4.0 bundle; the index covers ERP/CRM, connectivity, website, social media, cybersecurity, ICT skills and web sales only, and AI/cloud/IoT are mentioned in the survey description and discussion but excluded from the index. Limitations: 2019 reference year (pre-pandemic, before the 2021-2024 Istat AI modules), expert-based item selection, logical imputation. Relevance: RQ1 as official-data context on general digitalisation (manufacturing 0.356 vs Italy 0.369, services 0.399; size gradient 0.341/0.555/0.716; South 0.330, Islands 0.270) and RQ5 as an example of a composite index on Istat microdata that cannot be read as AI adoption. The coverage score stays at 2 (national probability sample, explicit NACE C row); date lowered to 1 because of the 2019 data.

authors: Bronzini, R.; Giunta, A.; Pierucci, E.; Sforza, M.
title: More technology, more loans? How advanced digital technologies influence firms' financing conditions
population: Italian manufacturing (incl. energy and extractive) and non-financial private service firms with at least 20 employees in the Bank of Italy Survey on Industrial and Service Firms (INVIND); balanced panel of about 2,200 limited liability firms 2015-2019 matched with Cerved balance sheets; construction excluded
geography: Italy (NUTS-2 fixed effects; sample 42% North-West, 20% North-East, 19% Centre, 19% South)
ai_definition: Adoption of at least one of six advanced digital technologies surveyed by INVIND since 2015: advanced robots, 3D printing, cloud computing, IoT, artificial intelligence, big data analytics (dummy 'At Least 1 DT', absorbing from first adoption). AI is grouped with cloud, IoT and big data in the 'Information DT' bundle and never isolated.
coi_note: Bank of Italy/MUR and Roma Tre authors; CC BY-NC-ND; data not shareable (Bank of Italy INVIND microdata).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Probit-2SLS endogenous-treatment model (plus Heckit for the self-reported credit-rationing item) on a balanced panel of about 2,200 INVIND firms with at least 20 employees (manufacturing and services), 2015-2019, matched with Cerved; instrument = use of the Industry 4.0 hyper-depreciation at t+1 (alternative IV: regional-sector DT investment exposure). AI is one of six INVIND technologies but is never measured on its own: the treatment is 'at least one DT' or the Information DT bundle (cloud, IoT, AI, big data), so no AI adoption rate is reported. Useful Italy-specific figures: 78% of large vs 69% of SMEs (20+ employees) adopted at least one DT; 59% of firms made no DT investment; adoption lowers credit rationing by 0.58 pp (Information DT 0.77 pp), raises leverage 4.2% and lowers debt cost 3.6%; in the manufacturing subsample only Operational DT (robots, 3D printing) reduces rationing (-0.17, 10% level) while leverage (+3.5%) and debt cost (-2.4%) effects hold; effects comparable for SMEs and large firms. Limitations: firms below 20 employees excluded (micro firms absent), self-reported rationing available only for applicants (723 obs.), bundle treatment, credit-rationing result not robust to the alternative IV. Relevance: RQ4 (financial-condition effects of Industry 4.0 adoption, causal design), RQ3 (access to finance as barrier eased by adoption; complementary investments), RQ1 (INVIND adoption shares by size), RQ5 (INVIND as a source family distinct from Istat).

org: Journal of Industrial and Business Economics
authors: Gahn, S. J.
title: Path dependence in the digital adoption process: a cross-section analysis of Italian firms with a special focus on the Apulia region
population: Italian firms in the Istat Permanent Business Census 2019 (reference year 2018, integrated with FRAME SBS), all sectors (NACE 4-digit controls); 201,465 firm-level observations, of which 44,555 answered the long questionnaire with the digital items, weighted to the universe; accessed at Istat ADELE laboratory
geography: Italy (20 regions plus the autonomous provinces of Bolzano and Trento), with a province-level analysis of Apulia
fieldwork_period: Census 2019, reference year 2018; past investment 2016-2018, planned investment 2019-2021
ai_definition: No AI-specific measure. Dependent variables: nine binary items on planned investment 2019-2021 in digital technologies (fibre-optic ultra-wideband, 4G-5G mobile, IoT, immersive technologies, big data, 'advanced automation, collaborative robots and intelligent systems', 3D printers, simulation between interconnected machines, cyber-security); path dependence = investment in the same technology in 2016-2018. AI is cited in the introduction but not isolated empirically.
coi_note: Single academic author (Niccolo Cusano University, Rome; previously Bari); PRIN 2017 Mezzogiorno, PON and Argentine PICT funding; no conflict of interest declared (p. 1).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Cross-sectional binomial logits on Istat Permanent Business Census microdata (reference 2018; 44,555 long-questionnaire respondents weighted to 201,465 firms, all sectors, ADELE laboratory) explaining planned 2019-2021 investment in nine digital technologies by past 2016-2018 investment in the same technology (path dependence) plus firm controls, region and, for Apulia, province dummies. AI is not measured separately: the closest item is the census bundle 'advanced automation, collaborative robots and intelligent systems'; no adoption shares are reported (only relative risk ratios) and no manufacturing or size-class breakdown is shown (NACE 4 sector dummies included but not displayed). Headline results: path dependence RRRs from 1.52 (fibre) to 134 (immersive) and 55.9 (automation/robots); past recruitment, R&D and digital investment intensity are enablers; relative size has RRR below 1 (author reads it as smaller firms more prone to plan adoption, a counter-intuitive result given the size variable is a within-sector sales share); Apulia and Sicily strongly penalised (Apulia RRR 0.06-0.72 vs Piedmont). Limitations: planned rather than realised adoption, cross-section, no manufacturing results, correction of the earlier coding: manufacturing_coverage set to none (sector controls only). Relevance: RQ3 (cumulative capabilities, prior digital and R&D investment and Southern location as enablers/barriers; same Istat census source family as the Istat precursor-technology analyses) and RQ5 (measurement via planned investment items). Published in the same journal targeted by the manuscript.

authors: Calabrese, G. G.; Falavigna, G.; Ippoliti, R.
title: Innovation policy and corporate finance: The Italian automotive supply chain and its transition to Industry 4.0
population: SMEs of the Italian automotive supply chain responding to the national survey of the Observatory on the Italian Automotive Supply Chain (Chamber of Commerce of Turin, ANFIA, CAMI Ca' Foscari), merged with AIDA accounts and Ceris Rating scores; pooled 2017-2019 sample of 1,241 firm-year observations (about 1,000 initial observations, halved to 448-690 in regressions by missing values and lags); 35.9% report access to the Calenda 4.0 incentives
ai_definition: No direct technology measure. Treatment = survey self-report of access to the Calenda 4.0 (Industry 4.0 Plan) incentives (interest-rate contribution +30% and Central Guarantee Fund guarantees up to 80% for SMEs, hyper-depreciation 250%, super-depreciation 120-140%, R&D tax relief 50%, productivity-bonus flat tax), used as proxy of investment in Industry 4.0 technologies (BDA, AI, ICT, IoT named in the framing).
coi_note: CNR-IRCrES, CAMI Ca' Foscari and University of Eastern Piedmont authors; the survey source (Observatory on the Italian Automotive Supply Chain) is co-run by CAMI, an affiliation of the first author, and Ceris Rating is a CNR-IRCrES product; no commercial interest in the policy evaluated.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Pooled OLS/logit and Heckman two-step on 2017-2019 survey data of the Observatory on the Italian Automotive Supply Chain merged with AIDA and Ceris Rating (1,241 firm-years, 35.9% with self-reported access to Calenda 4.0 incentives; regressions on 448-690 observations). Access to the incentives, interacted with the lagged outcome, is associated with a 0.25-0.29 higher log financial debt ratio (p<0.05/0.01), 2.4-2.5 times the odds of positive profit and about +0.01 on log ROS/ROI/ROE. Abstract-based figures were confirmed; sample, period and data sources are now recorded. AI is not measured: the treatment is self-reported access to the whole Calenda 4.0 package (guarantees, interest contributions, hyper/super depreciation), used as a proxy for Industry 4.0 investment; AI is only named among the target technologies. Limitations: correlational design on an unbalanced pooled sample without panel or matching estimators (authors state they cannot confirm causality), survey self-selection, single supply chain (85% components producers), effects concentrated among better-rated SMEs. Relevance: RQ3 (financial constraints and public guarantees as enablers for manufacturing SMEs) and RQ4 (self-reported access to incentives associated with better financial performance, non-causal).

org: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
authors: Marioni, L. da S.; Rincon-Aznar, A.; Venturini, F.
title: Productivity performance, distance to frontier and AI innovation: Firm-level evidence from Europe
population: Firms in 15 European countries (Italy: 208 firms, 27 AI innovators) drawn from ORBIS Europe balance sheets and matched to OECD REGPAT patents; treated = 284 firms filing a first AI patent 2011-2019, controls = 1,205 never-AI-patenting firms selected by propensity score matching (10 nearest neighbours)
geography: 15 European countries (Austria, Belgium, Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, UK)
fieldwork_period: 2011-2019 (ORBIS Europe balance sheets; OECD REGPAT release January 2021)
ai_definition: AI measured on its own but as innovation, not adoption: treatment dummy equal to one from the year of the firm's first AI patent filing onwards, AI patents identified by the CPC codes of Meniere et al. (2017) in OECD REGPAT; firms patenting in robotics and additive manufacturing are excluded from controls and used as alternative treatment. No use/adoption item; predictive and generative AI not distinguished.
coi_note: Academic authors (NIESR, CMA, Urbino, Lund); H2020 Untangled funding; CC-BY article; authors declare no competing interests (p. 16).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Staggered DiD (LP-DiD event study plus distance-to-frontier regressions) on 1,489 ORBIS Europe firms from 15 countries, 2011-2019, where treatment is the first AI patent filing identified in OECD REGPAT via CPC codes; 284 AI innovators vs 1,205 PSM controls. AI is isolated from the rest of the Industry 4.0 bundle (robotics and additive manufacturing patentees are excluded from controls and used as a placebo treatment, which turns out negative), but the measure captures AI production, not use or adoption; no survey item. Italy contributes 208 firms (27 AI innovators, Table A.5) and no Italy-specific or sector-specific effect is estimated, although roughly half of the AI innovators are in manufacturing divisions (machinery 41, computer/electronics 38, electrical equipment 23, motor vehicles 18, Table A.6). Limitations acknowledged: small number of AI patentees, ORBIS under-sampling of small firms (employment weights used), indirect catch-up effect fragile to matching choices, no distinction between predictive and generative AI. Relevance: RQ4 (causal productivity premium of AI innovation, 6.2-17% event study, 2.1-6% DTF, with laggards benefiting slightly more) and RQ5 (patent-based measurement as a source family distinct from Istat/Eurostat adoption surveys). Not usable for RQ1 adoption rates.

org: Economics of Innovation and New Technology
authors: Bratta, B.; Romano, L.; Acciari, P.; Mazzolari, F.
title: Assessing the impact of digital technology diffusion policies. Evidence from Italy
population: Entire population of Italian limited liability companies: 2018 corporate tax returns (tax year 2017, MEF) linked to 2016 Bureau van Dijk balance sheets and ANPAL hirings/separations 2016-Q1 2019 (381,623 firms, of which 6,553 hyper-depreciation users); 7,607 beneficiaries observed in tax returns for the take-up analysis; a sub-sample of 16,135 firms with 10+ employees (791 beneficiaries) merged with the ISTAT 2018 ICT survey
geography: Italy (20 regions; North-West, North-East, Centre, South breakdown)
fieldwork_period: Tax year 2017 (incentive introduced by the 2017 Budget Law); employment outcomes January 2017 to March 2019 vs 2016 baseline
ai_definition: No AI item. Treatment = use of the 2017 hyper-depreciation (iperammortamento, notional +150% of cost) for tangible Industry 4.0 goods (machine tools, robots, 3D printing, warehouse systems, monitoring and inspection equipment, human-machine interfaces, interconnected to the firm IT systems). Digital maturity classes built from the ISTAT 2018 ICT survey (ERP/CRM/SCM, ICT specialists, investment in at least two among IoT, additive manufacturing, advanced robotics, cloud, big data analytics, AR/VR in 2014-2016).
coi_note: Two authors at the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance (Direzione Studi e Ricerche Economico Fiscali), the administration that designed the incentive, and two at Centro Studi Confindustria (employers' association that lobbied for Industry 4.0 incentives); ex-post evaluation by policy stakeholders. The paper declares no conflict of interest.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Journal version (EINT 32(8), 1114-1137) of the MEF working paper already in the catalog as bratta2020hyperdep; all figures now verified on the journal PDF, so this record supersedes the WP for citation. The paper links the universe of Italian limited liability companies (381,623 firms, 6,553 hyper-depreciation users; 7,607 users in the tax returns) across MEF tax returns, Bureau van Dijk balance sheets, ANPAL job flows and the ISTAT 2018 ICT survey, estimates 2017 take-up (3.8 to 7.0 billion euro, 56% of beneficiaries and 83% of investment in manufacturing, 82% of beneficiaries micro or small), profiles beneficiaries (ex-ante more productive, 45% of firms with 10+ employees at zero digital maturity in 2016) and estimates PSM difference-in-differences employment effects (+3.0 p.p. hirings, +7 p.p. total employment, rising with firm size, +2.93 p.p. hirings in manufacturing only). AI is not measured separately: the treatment is the Industry 4.0 tangible-goods bundle (machine tools, robots, interconnected equipment) and the digital maturity index pools IoT, robotics, cloud, big data and AR/VR; no AI item. Limitations: single incentive wave (2017), universal eligibility so identification relies on PSM on observables, attenuation from late deliveries, no general-equilibrium or productivity outcomes, authors from the policy owner (MEF) and Confindustria. Relevance: RQ1 (size and sector skew of Industry 4.0 take-up, 2016 digital maturity distribution), RQ3 (fiscal incentives as enabler, pre-existing performance as a selection factor), RQ4 (quasi-causal positive employment effects of subsidised digital investment, heterogeneous by size), RQ5 (administrative data as an alternative measurement source).

authors: Nucci, F.; Puccioni, C.; Ricchi, O.
title: Digital technologies and productivity: A firm-level investigation
population: Italian enterprises with at least 10 employees responding to the digitalisation module of the ISTAT 2019 Permanent Census of Enterprises (reference 2016-2018), merged with ASIA and SBS Frame balance-sheet data; 108,682 respondents, of which 90,159 used at least one digital technology and enter the latent-class model
fieldwork_period: Census survey May-October 2019 (technologies adopted 2016-2018); productivity change 2015-2018
ai_definition: No stand-alone AI measure. Treatment = intensive digital adoption: firm belongs to ISTAT latent classes 3 ('experimenting innovative IT solutions') or 4 ('digitally mature'), built from 11 dichotomous technology items for 2016-2018 (business software, cloud, fibre, 4G-5G, IoT, immersive tech, big data, 'Advanced automation functions, Collaborative robots and Intelligent systems', 3D printing, simulation, cyber security). AI is subsumed under 'intelligent systems'.
coi_note: Authors at Sapienza and MEF Treasury; uses ISTAT microdata; no policy being self-evaluated.
notes: Figures and page numbers refer to the MEF Department of the Treasury Working Paper No. 3, April 2022 (same title plus 'for Italy', same authors), which is the openly available version; the Economic Modelling article (CC-BY, vol. 128, 106524) could not be downloaded from this network (ScienceDirect and Sapienza IRIS blocked). Numbers may differ marginally in the published version. Not AI-specific: 'treated' = ISTAT digital maturity classes 3-4. The 29/45/22/4 class shares are ISTAT population shares quoted by the authors.

authors: Antonietti, R.; Cattani, L.; Pedrini, G.
title: Robots and the productivity of local manufacturing systems in Emilia-Romagna: the mediating role of occupational similarity and complexity
population: Manufacturing sectors (15 two-digit NACE groups) in the 39 local labour market areas of Emilia-Romagna; area-industry-year cells built from SILER administrative employer-employee data (universe of manufacturing firms), AIDA balance sheets (about 6,000 firms), IFR World Robotics 2020 robot installations and the INAPP-ISTAT ICP task survey
ai_definition: No AI item. Exposure to industrial robots: ROBDEN = yearly IFR robot installations in Italian manufacturing sectors allocated to Emilia-Romagna LLMA-sector cells with 2008 employment weights, divided by 2008 FTE employment in the cell. The conclusions explicitly leave AI and IoT to future research.
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova, GSSI, Kore Enna); disclosure statement reports no conflict of interest (p.23).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Two-step panel analysis (fixed effects with cluster and Driscoll-Kraay SE, plus 2SLS with robot density in seven European countries as instruments) on 39 LLMAs x 15 manufacturing sectors of Emilia-Romagna, 2008-2017, combining IFR robot installations (shift-share allocation with 2008 employment weights), SILER administrative employment data, AIDA balance sheets and INAPP-ISTAT ICP task data. AI is not measured at all: the exposure variable is industrial robots only, and the authors explicitly list AI and IoT as future extensions. Main numbers: no significant effect of robot density on value added per FTE at any lag; employment elasticity -0.074 after three years (p<0.05), concentrated in high-routine jobs; the employment loss is significant only in low-similarity (-0.110) or high-complexity (-0.092) LLMAs and outside industrial districts (-0.092 vs -0.042 inside). Limitations: area-industry cells, not firms; robot installations imputed from national sectoral data; one region; pre-2018 period. Relevant to RQ4 (employment and productivity effects of automation in an Italian manufacturing region, correlational with IV check) and RQ3 (industrial districts and occupational structure as moderators); marginal for RQ1/RQ2 since no adoption rates are reported.

authors: Cirillo, V.; Fanti, L.; Mina, A.; Ricci, A.
title: The adoption of digital technologies: Investment, skills, work organisation
population: Italian firms with at least 5 employees in non-agricultural private sectors, INAPP RIL survey waves 2015 and 2018 (partial panel; each wave covers over 30,000 firms); estimation panel about 8,000 firms per year, 7,746 observations in the main models
ai_definition: No AI item. I4.0 adoption = answer to 'In the period 2015-2017 did the firm invest in these new technologies?' with options Internet of things, Robotics, Big data analytics, Augmented reality, Cybersecurity (multiple answers); outcomes: at least one technology (dummy) and number of technologies (0-5).
coi_note: Academic and INAPP authors; INAPP runs the RIL survey.
notes: Full text read (publisher PDF obtained from the Zenodo CC-BY deposit, record 10425139). Distinct from cirillo2023digital (Industry and Innovation) already in the catalog, although same RIL data. Key value for the paper: a depth measure (single vs multi-technology adoption) and the 39.1% investment rate for firms >=5 employees versus 26% for firms >=1 employee, a population-threshold effect relevant to RQ5. The Table 4 family-firm split by sector was read from a two-column PDF layout and should be double-checked against the original table before citing.

org: Journal of Quality in Maintenance Engineering
authors: Stefanini, R.; Tancredi, G. P. C.; Vignali, G.; Monica, L.
title: Industry 4.0 and intelligent predictive maintenance: a survey about the advantages and constraints in the Italian context
population: Italian companies (mixed sizes and sectors, food industry over-represented at 32.9%) selected from the Kompass database; 1,000 contacted by e-mail, 70 respondents
fieldwork_period: not stated (questionnaire open 4 weeks; article received December 2021)
ai_definition: Industry 4.0 key enabling technologies rated on a 1-5 implementation scale (additive manufacturing, big data, AR, VR, collaborative robots, IoT, machine learning, AGV, cloud, cyber security, digital twin); machine learning is one of 11 items but no ML adoption rate is reported; 'intelligent predictive maintenance' = sensor-based monitoring to diagnose and prevent faults.
coi_note: University of Parma with INAIL (public insurer); no funding declared. INAIL co-authorship signals occupational-safety framing but no commercial interest.
notes: Full text read (Emerald CC-BY PDF). Published in vol. 29 no. 5 (2023) pp. 37-49, online August 2022: batch file lists 2022, id uses the print year 2023. Very small opt-in sample (n=70, about 7% response), non-representative, food industry 33%; percentages are not generalisable. The abstract reports 37% IPdM while the text (p.44) reports 34.2%; use 34.2% with the caveat. ML is listed among the 11 KETs but no ML rate is published (Fig. 5 only).

authors: Cugno, M.; Castagnoli, R.; Büchi, G.; Pini, M.
title: Industry 4.0 and production recovery in the covid era
population: Italian manufacturing SMEs with 5-249 employees (NACE C, 24 divisions) from the Unioncamere end-2020 representative survey of 3,000 manufacturing firms with 5-499 employees (CATI); 2,925 SMEs, of which 2,622 stopped activity during the pandemic are analysed
ai_definition: Openness to Industry 4.0 = count (0-11) of technologies implemented among advanced manufacturing, additive manufacturing, augmented reality, big data, cloud, cyber security, IoT, simulation, horizontal/vertical integration, artificial intelligence, blockchain (MISE 2017 list plus blockchain and AI). AI is one of the 11 dummies; no separate AI rate reported.
coi_note: University of Turin with Centro Studi Tagliacarne (Unioncamere research centre, data owner).
notes: Full text read (PMC copy of the Elsevier article, Wayback snapshot). Outcome is perceived (expected) recovery, self-reported, not measured production. Adoption share 13.4% is computed from 351/2,622 (not stated as a percentage in the text). Same Unioncamere survey family as pini2019south and cugno2021barriers.

authors: Di Maria, E.; De Marchi, V.; Galeazzo, A.
title: Industry 4.0 technologies and circular economy: The mediating role of supply chain integration
population: Italian manufacturing firms in Made in Italy industries (automotive, rubber and plastics, electronic appliances, lighting, furniture, eyewear, jewelry, sport equipment, textile and clothing) with turnover above 1 million euro, located in six Northern regions (Veneto, Friuli-Venezia Giulia, Trentino-Alto Adige, Lombardia, Piemonte, Emilia-Romagna); AIDA population 7,694; 1,229 respondents (16 per cent); 189 adopters of at least one I4.0 technology analysed
ai_definition: Two formative constructs built from yes/no application of each technology across seven value-chain activities (index 1-7 per technology): data processing technologies = big data; cloud computing and IoT; RFID and sensors in the product; smart manufacturing technologies = robotics, additive manufacturing, 3D scanner, augmented reality. AI is named in the conceptual definition of data processing technologies but is not a measured item.
coi_note: University of Padova authors; funded by a University of Padova BIRD grant.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). PLS-SEM (with covariance SEM robustness check) on the 189 Industry 4.0 adopters within the 2017 Padova CAWI survey (May-December 2017) of 7,694 Made in Italy manufacturers with turnover above 1 million euro in six Northern regions (1,229 respondents, 16 per cent response rate). The abstract-based record set sample_n to 1,200: the analysed sample is 189 adopters, so sample_n is corrected to 189 (the 1,229 respondents are kept in population); the implied adopter share is about 15.4 per cent. AI is not measured: it appears only in the conceptual description of data processing technologies, whose measured items are big data, cloud/IoT and RFID/sensors, each scored by number of value-chain activities (mean 1.02 of 7 among adopters, versus 1.69 for smart manufacturing). Limitations: adopter-only, Northern Italy and Made in Italy sectors, self-reported CE outcomes, cross-sectional. Relevance: RQ1 (2017 adoption baseline in Northern manufacturing; data processing technologies less diffused than automation), RQ4 (self-reported CE effects, data technologies with weaker direct effect and no SCI mediation), RQ5 (same 2017 survey reused in capestro2024exploiting, bettiol2022ict, demarchi2020circular; counts of papers overstate independent evidence).

authors: Chiarini, A.; Kumar, M.
title: What is Quality 4.0? An exploratory sequential mixed methods study of Italian manufacturing companies
population: Phase 1: 21 quality managers of Italian B2B manufacturing companies with more than 50 employees that implemented I4.0 in the previous three years; Phase 2: quality managers of 3,865 large and medium ISO 9001-certified B2B manufacturers (consultancy client list), 282 returned, 216 retained (122 large, 94 medium)
ai_definition: No adoption rate. AI appears as one of 11 Quality 4.0 themes rated on a 1-5 agreement scale: 'Use of artificial intelligence and predictive software for problem-solving and prevention of product failure/nonconformity' (variable PREDIC).
coi_note: Sampling frame supplied by an operations-management consulting company; respondents pre-screened for I4.0 knowledge; attitudinal, not behavioural, data.
notes: Full text read on the author accepted manuscript (Cardiff ORCA eprint 142174, Wayback copy); page numbers are AAM pages, not journal pages 4890-4910. Published online 24 June 2021, print vol. 60 no. 16 (2022). The study does NOT report AI use rates: only agreement that AI/predictive software should be part of a Quality 4.0 model. Small/medium firms under 50 employees excluded by design.

authors: Cimini, C.; Boffelli, A.; Lagorio, A.; Kalchschmidt, M.; Pinto, R.
title: How do industry 4.0 technologies influence organisational change? An empirical analysis of Italian SMEs
population: Ten manufacturing SMEs in northern Italy (fewer than 200 employees, turnover below 50 million euro) selected by judgemental sampling with a local Confindustria branch (Bergamo area)
ai_definition: No AI item. Six I4.0 technologies rated on a six-stage implementation scale (non-use, orientation, preparation, testing, routine, refinement and integration): advanced manufacturing solutions, advanced robotics, augmented reality, IoT and big data, simulation, cyber security.
coi_note: University of Bergamo; case access via Confindustria Bergamo.
notes: Full text read on the author accepted manuscript (University of Bergamo Aisberg repository, Wayback copy); page numbers are AAM pages, not journal pages 695-721. Published online April 2020, print vol. 32 no. 3 (2021). Qualitative, ten cases, no AI; useful for RQ3 (lean prerequisites) and RQ4 (job profiles, competences).

org: Competitiveness Review: An International Business Journal
authors: Pagano, A.; Carloni, E.; Galvani, S.; Bocconcelli, R.
title: The dissemination mechanisms of Industry 4.0 knowledge in traditional industrial districts: evidence from Italy
population: Pesaro industrial district (furniture and woodworking machinery, Marche): 18 in-depth interviews with firms, institutions, consultants and university staff, plus mapping of 83 I4.0 dissemination initiatives 2014-2019
ai_definition: No adoption measure. Object = diffusion of Industry 4.0 related knowledge (IoT, machine learning expertise, digital projects) in a traditional district.
coi_note: University of Urbino authors; CC-BY article.
notes: Full text read (Emerald CC-BY PDF). Single-district qualitative case (Pesaro, Marche); evidence on districts as a determinant is narrative, not statistical. Online May 2020, print vol. 31 no. 1 (2021).

authors: Chiarini, A.; Belvedere, V.; Grando, A.
title: Industry 4.0 strategies and technological developments. An exploratory research from Italian manufacturing companies
population: Operations managers of Italian industrial companies with at least one manufacturing plant, drawn from a Chamber of Commerce database of around 7,000 companies; 200 usable questionnaires (74 engineering/mechanical, 63 continuous process, 29 electronics, 34 others)
fieldwork_period: online survey over the 12 months preceding submission (submitted 3 July 2019, so approximately mid-2018 to mid-2019); exact dates not stated
ai_definition: No AI item. Seven Industry 4.0 technologies rated on a 1-4 implementation scale (will not implement / considering / project under way / project completed): big data analytics, digital supply chain, IoT, cloud computing, robotics, 3D printing, AGVs. Big data analytics is the only data-analytics item and is measured separately.
coi_note: Verona, Cattolica and Bocconi authors; no conflict declared. First author also runs a consulting firm active in Industry 4.0 (notes on contributors).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Opt-in online survey of operations managers in 200 Italian manufacturing companies (frame: about 7,000 Chamber of Commerce records, implied response about 3 per cent, fieldwork in the 12 months before July 2019), with 95 per cent CI tests on Likert means and ANOVA between adopters and others, plus open-ended comments.
