AI is not an item: the only analytics item is 'big data analytics', measured separately on a 1-4 implementation scale (16 per cent completed, 34 per cent will not implement), the lowest completed share after 3D printing and AGVs, and the only technology with no significant link to any strategic objective. Limitations: non-probability sample, no response rate stated, self-reported perceptions, size breakdown collected but not reported. Relevance: RQ1 (technology-level adoption rates in Italian manufacturing circa 2018-2019, with big data analytics as a proxy for data-driven AI), RQ3 (qualitative barriers: legacy machines and protocols, skills, cost, worker resistance, supply-chain bargaining power), RQ5 (opt-in managerial survey vs official statistics; also quotes the MISE 2018 figure of 8.4 per cent of Italian companies implementing I4.0 at end 2017).

authors: Cassetta, E.; Monarca, U.; Dileo, I.; Di Berardino, C.; Pini, M.
title: The relationship between digital technologies and internationalisation. Evidence from Italian SMEs
population: Italian SMEs (1-249 employees) from all macro-sectors (agriculture, manufacturing, construction, trade, hotels and restaurants, other services) in the Si.Camera-Unioncamere 2015 survey; cross-section of 2,516 firms representative of about 3.7 million enterprises with at least one person employed
geography: Italy (macro-regions North-West, North-East, Centre, South and Islands)
ai_definition: Not AI or Industry 4.0: binary items on e-commerce DTs (website, online selling, social network), e-business DTs (sharing supply-chain information with suppliers via internet, cloud computing) and digital skills (digital training, ICT competencies), plus product, process/organisational and marketing innovation; probit on export propensity.
coi_note: Academic authors plus Marco Pini (Unioncamere-Si.Camera, views stated as personal); no conflict of interest reported (p. 23).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Probit models with marginal effects at means on a 2015 Unioncamere-Si.Camera cross-section of 2,516 Italian SMEs (all sectors, 1-249 employees, representative of 3.7 million enterprises) relating export status to e-commerce DTs (website, online selling, social media), e-business DTs (electronic sharing with suppliers, cloud) and digital skills, with interactions with process/organisational innovation. No AI and no Industry 4.0 measure: the paper predates the AI items and is peripheral to criterion a; manufacturing enters only as a sector dummy (largest export propensity, +17 to +21 pp). Italy-specific baseline figures from 2015 are useful as a pre-Industry 4.0 benchmark of SME digital maturity: cloud 2.0%, digital training 2.0%, ICT competencies 12.0%, online selling 3.2%, website 45.7%. Headline results: website +4.7 to +5.4 pp and online selling +3.3 pp on export probability; e-business DTs matter only when combined with process/organisational innovation (+1.7 pp interaction) and ICT skills x organisational innovation (+2.5 pp); cloud never significant. Limitations: cross-section, self-reported binary items, correlational (acknowledged). Relevance: RQ3 (complementarity of skills and organisational change as enablers; skills gap in micro and small firms) and RQ4 (self-reported performance association, not causal); RQ5 as an example of the Unioncamere source family. Low priority for citation.

authors: Scarpino, C.; Tumino, A.; Salvadori, G.; Vadruccio, R.
title: Evaluating Industry 5.0 Adoption: Insights on Industrial IoT and Sustainability in Italian Manufacturing
population: Italian medium-sized and large manufacturing enterprises surveyed by the Internet of Things Observatory of Politecnico di Milano (CAWI); 162 companies (110 large, 52 medium) plus 19 interviews
ai_definition: Industrial IoT adoption (at least one IIoT project) and knowledge/awareness of Industry 4.0/5.0 solutions, from a 33-question CAWI; interest in the Transition 5.0 Plan. No AI-specific item.
coi_note: Authors from the Politecnico di Milano IoT Observatory, which is partly financed by partner companies; survey run by the Observatory.
notes: Full text read (publisher OA PDF, Wayback copy of the Politecnico di Milano IRIS file; vol. 277, pp. 685-694; printed page = PDF page + 684). Conference paper (ISM 2025) with thin reporting of survey results: no adoption percentages are given beyond the Transition 5.0 interest figures (which the authors themselves call unreliable); most of the paper is a scenario model of CO2 savings and NPV. Non-probability sample skewed to large firms. Use mainly for RQ3 (policy barriers to Transition 5.0) and as context on the 2024 Transition 5.0 Plan.

authors: Nevi, G.; Bartoloni, S.; Pascucci, F.; Dezi, L.
title: Harnessing AI Capacities for Sustainable Business Models: Empowering Firms across Economic, Social, and Environmental Dimensions
population: CEOs and senior managers of 11 Italian cosmetics companies drawn from the Cosmetica Italia database, purposively selected for demonstrable sustainability commitment (certifications) and AI application in the business model; mix of large international firms and innovative startups
fieldwork_period: Key informants identified between December 2023 and February 2024; online interviews conducted February to April 2024 (the text gives both windows)
ai_definition: AI capacities (perceptive, predictive, prescriptive) conceptualised as lower-order technological capabilities that strengthen dynamic capabilities (sensing, seizing, reconfiguring); AI adoption in the business model was a sampling criterion, not a measured variable; no adoption rate or scale; AI solutions named by firms are machine learning, predictive analytics, NLP, NLG, computer-vision quality control.
coi_note: Academic authors (Universita Politecnica delle Marche, Mercatorum, Sapienza); no funding or conflict declared.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Qualitative study: 11 semi-structured online interviews (about 45 minutes, early 2024) with CEOs and senior managers of Italian cosmetics firms purposively selected from the Cosmetica Italia database because they already combine sustainability certifications and AI use, triangulated with company documents; thematic coding on the dynamic-capabilities framework (sensing, seizing, reconfiguring) and the three business-model dimensions. AI IS the explicit object (perceptive, predictive, prescriptive capacities) but it is a sampling criterion, not a measured variable: no adoption rate, no scale, no effect sizes; Table I (firm characteristics) is an image not captured in the text layer. Limitations: adopter-only, single sector, no quantitative evidence, self-reported benefits (waste, returns) without figures. The abstract-based coding was correct; the full text adds concrete AI functions (camera-based quality control on the line, NLP for CRM, NLG for localisation, predictive algorithms for packaging and loyalty) and barriers (SME skills and data gap, job-loss fears, AI washing, energy footprint). Relevance: RQ2 (functions in a manufacturing-heavy consumer sector where Italy makes 67% of European makeup) and RQ3 (barriers), with a measurement caveat for RQ5.

authors: Bravi, L.; Pierli, G.; Murmura, F.; Musso, F.
title: Integrating Industry 4.0 and Industry 5.0: a study of hybrid adoption in SMEs and its impact on sustainability, human-centricity, resilience
population: Italian micro, small and medium enterprises in the automotive sector (ATECO/NACE 29) with an email address in the ATOKA database: 1,192 identified, 859 valid contacts, 78 respondents, of which 46 declared Industry 4.0/5.0 adoption and formed the regression and cluster sample; plus one micro-firm case study (2 interviews)
geography: Italy (firms headquartered in Italy; case-study firm in Northern Italy)
fieldwork_period: May-June 2023 (email survey with one reminder after two weeks); follow-up case-study interviews after the quantitative phase
ai_definition: AI is not measured separately: it is one component of a single Industry 4.0 item, 'Digitization (Simulation, Digital Twins, Artificial Intelligence, Augmented Reality, Virtual Reality or mixed technology)', rated on a 1-5 adoption scale together with 8 other I4.0 items and 10 I5.0 items. The regression predictor is an AdoptionScore (0-2) summing two binary indicators, 'High 4.0 adoption' and 'High 5.0 adoption'.
coi_note: Academic authors (University of Urbino); partially funded by MIMIT, FSC project 'Pesaro CTE SQUARE'; no conflict declared.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Email survey (May-June 2023) of Italian automotive SMEs (ATECO 29) drawn from ATOKA: 1,192 identified, 859 contacted, 78 respondents (about 9%), of which only the 46 self-declared Industry 4.0/5.0 adopters enter the OLS regressions (item-by-item, predictor = AdoptionScore 0-2) and the K-means clustering; one micro-firm case study adds qualitative depth. AI is NOT measured separately: it sits inside a single 'Digitization' item that bundles simulation, digital twins, AI, AR and VR (cluster means 3.63/2.75/3.39 on a 1-5 scale), so no AI adoption rate can be derived. Limitations: tiny, purposive, self-selected sample (Strivers n=4), self-reported Likert outcomes, bivariate OLS per item without controls, cross-sectional; the abstract-based coding was correct but did not reveal that 41% of respondents had made no I4.0 investment and that effects are driven by sustainability items. Relevance: RQ1 (depth of I4.0 adoption in automotive SMEs, 41% non-investors), RQ3 (funding and skills barriers, agility and culture as enablers, size moderation), RQ4 (self-reported association between hybrid adoption and sustainability/human-centricity, null on resilience), RQ5 (example of AI absorbed into a technology bundle, non-comparable with institutional AI indicators).

org: International Journal of Logistics Research and Applications
authors: Modica, T.; Colicchia, C.; Tappia, E.; Klumpp, M.
title: Sizing the roles: an exploratory research about Logistics 4.0 diffusion
population: 65 Italian firms (34 large, 31 SMEs) from the Contract Logistics Observatory network of Politecnico di Milano: 39 manufacturers, 14 logistics service providers, 12 retailers; purposive sampling, 475 contacted, 14% response
ai_definition: Logistics 4.0 (L40) diffusion measured through the technologies adopted (advanced automation, mobile systems, vertical/horizontal integration software, digital platforms, advanced analytics including AI and digital twin), application areas, drivers, and a two-dimensional maturity model (horizontal: Visibility & Monitoring, Planning & Control, Predictability & Optimization; vertical: number of principles Automation, Integration, Intelligence).
coi_note: Authors from Politecnico di Milano Contract Logistics Observatory (partner-funded) and Göttingen; sample drawn from the Observatory's contacts.
notes: Version read: accepted manuscript from the Politecnico di Milano repository (41 pages, tables at the end; Wayback Save Page Now capture); page numbers refer to the manuscript PDF, not to the journal pagination (vol. 29 no. 6, pp. 753-775; online 2025). Mixed population: 60% manufacturers, the rest LSPs and retailers; results are not split by sector. Relevant depth indicator: only 12% of firms reach the predictive/optimisation stage, where AI/advanced analytics sit; no firm combines all three principles. Interviewees pre-selected for high L40 awareness, so adoption is over-stated relative to the population.

authors: Cosma, A. M. I.; Silvestri, L.; Coloca, A.; Filice, L.
title: How Industry 4.0 is shaping the future of a disadvantaged region: The case of Calabria
population: 20 Calabrian manufacturing SMEs (different manufacturing sectors) that had recently started Industry 4.0 technological innovation initiatives; interviewees were business owners and key decision-makers; profile: 5 firms <15 employees, 13 with 15-100, 2 with >100; 6 with <2.5 million euro turnover, 10 with 2.5-15 million, 4 with >15 million
fieldwork_period: not stated (paper presented at the 6th International Conference on Industry 4.0 and Smart Manufacturing, published 2025)
ai_definition: No AI measure. Industry 4.0 investments made under the Italian Industry 4.0 legislation (number of I4.0 machines or assets per firm); motivations and short and medium-long term effects as perceived by entrepreneurs, coded by thematic and content analysis (keyword frequencies).
coi_note: Academic authors (University Niccolo Cusano Rome and University of Calabria); no funding or sponsor disclosed.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Qualitative study: 20 interviews (about 25 minutes each) with owners and decision-makers of Calabrian manufacturing SMEs that had invested in Industry 4.0 assets, analysed by thematic and content analysis with keyword frequencies (percentages of the 20 firms). AI is not measured: the object is the Industry 4.0 investment bundle (machines or assets under the Italian plan); data analysis and predictive maintenance appear only as marginal themes (5% each). The full text refines the abstract: process improvement is cited by 100% of firms and tax incentives by 45%, whereas business efficiency and predictive maintenance (listed as relevant in the abstract) were each cited by one firm. Main barriers: bureaucracy and compliance (35%), staff training (20%), costs (10%); 70% foresee no long-term disadvantage. Limitations: tiny purposive sample, no fieldwork dates, no sectoral detail, descriptive percentages without inferential analysis, conference paper. Relevance: Mezzogiorno evidence on motivations and barriers (RQ3, role of incentives) and on self-reported effects (RQ4); marginal for RQ2 (data analysis as a use case) and for RQ5 as an example of small-n qualitative sources.

authors: Zoppelletto, A.; Santini, E.; Rossignoli, C.; Ricciardi, F.
title: Interfirm Collaboration Enhancing Twin Transition: Evidence From the Italian Fashion Industry
population: Manufacturing fashion firms (leather, clothing, textile, jewellery, eyewear) in north-eastern Italy: population of 1,262 firms from AIDA (Bureau van Dijk); 189 respondents (15% response rate), 30.7% micro, 40.3% small, 23.8% medium, 5.3% large; respondents mainly CEOs (63%) and COOs (31%)
fieldwork_period: Survey designed September-November 2021 with SMACT; CAWI survey administered by UniCredit Bank December 2021 to January 2022; six 90-minute triangulation interviews
ai_definition: AI not measured. Variables: external pressures for technology adoption (4 items: client requests, supplier requests, fiscal benefits or government incentives, supply chain projects, 1-5), collaboration along the supply chain because of digital technologies (single item), use of data for environmental purposes (single item), company dimension by 2019 turnover (micro-small, medium, large). AI appears only as an example of digital technologies in the introduction.
coi_note: Academic authors (Verona, Trento, Turin); work supported by the SMACT Competence Center and by UniCredit Bank, which also administered the survey. No vendor interest in AI, but the bank-channel sampling is a selection concern.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). CAWI survey of north-eastern Italian fashion manufacturers (leather, clothing, textile, jewellery, eyewear) designed with the SMACT competence centre and administered by UniCredit Bank in December 2021-January 2022: 1,262 firms in the AIDA frame, 189 respondents (15%), mostly micro and small, answered by CEOs/COOs; moderated mediation (PROCESS model 7, 5,000 bootstraps) with external pressure for technology adoption (4 items) -> collaboration enabled by digital technologies (single item) -> use of data for environmental purposes (single item), size by 2019 turnover as moderator. AI is NOT measured and digital technology adoption itself is not measured as a rate: the constructs are perceptual pressures and uses; AI is only cited as an example. Tables I-IV (loadings, correlations, coefficients) are images not captured in the text layer, so only the coefficients quoted in the prose (0.99/0.88/0.64) are available. Limitations: self-selected bank-channel sample, single-item mediator and outcome, cross-sectional, no causality, no AI content. The abstract-based coding was correct but lacked n=189, period, sector and size shares. Relevance: RQ3 (external pressure, incentives and supply-chain collaboration as enablers for SMEs; size moderation) and RQ5 (illustrates how 'digital/twin transition' surveys in Italian districts measure attitudes rather than adoption, hence non-comparable with AI indicators). No RQ1/RQ2/RQ4 content.

org: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
authors: Ferraro, G.; Quinto, I.; Scandurra, G.; Thomas, A.
title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence and Sustainability Management on Fostering ESG Practices and Competitive Perspectives Among SMEs
population: SMEs enrolled in the Italian register of Innovative SMEs and located in Lazio (population 394, 355 with contacts; random sample of 200); respondents 76% services, 17% manufacturing, 7% trade; 63% with 0-9 employees
ai_definition: Latent 'Artificial intelligence' construct measured by two 5-point Likert items that do not name AI: 'Digitalization' (the SME implements digitalization as a driver of sustainable business models, products and services) and 'Innovation management' (the SME adopts tools and methods supporting the innovation process). In the text AI is described as 'the capacity of SMEs to adopt digital technologies that support AI'. No AI technology, use case or adoption rate is measured.
coi_note: Academic authors (Tor Vergata, Parthenope); no funding or commercial interest stated.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). PLS-SEM (SmartPLS 4, 6,000 bootstraps) on 163 innovative SMEs located in Lazio (random sample of 200 out of 355 contactable firms in the regional register, 81% response, end of 2024); 76% services, 17% manufacturing (27 firms), 63% micro firms. Although the paper is framed around AI, the 'Artificial intelligence' latent variable is measured by two Likert items on digitalisation and innovation management that do not mention AI at all, so the study does not measure AI adoption, neither on its own nor as part of an Industry 4.0 bundle, and reports no adoption rate; outcomes (ESG pillars, competitive perspectives) are perceptual, with no control variables (authors' own limitation). The accuracy score is kept at 1 because the construct does not match its label, and the SM construct has Cronbach alpha 0.353. The abstract-based coding was not wrong but the AI definition is now known to be a mislabelled digitalisation construct. Relevance: marginal; RQ5 only as an example of how loosely 'AI' is operationalised in part of the Italian SME literature, RQ4 only as perceptual association (AI construct -> competitive perspectives 0.59). Not suitable for any claim about AI adoption in Italian manufacturing.

authors: Vadruccio, R.; Scarpino, C.; Tumino, A.
title: Unveiling Industrial Internet of Things potential for sustainable manufacturing: A Triple Bottom Line approach
population: Italian manufacturing companies that implemented IIoT projects; CAWI survey, 46 companies after cleaning, plus 15 interviews
ai_definition: Implementation of Industrial IoT projects in the factory and self-assessed Triple Bottom Line (economic, environmental, social) performance improvements; outcome = perceived value generated by the IIoT project (binary). No AI item.
coi_note: Authors from the Politecnico di Milano IoT Observatory (partner-funded).
notes: Full text read (publisher OA PDF via the Politecnico di Milano repository, Wayback capture; vol. 253, pp. 1083-1092; printed page = PDF page + 1082; page 1 carries a duplicated header watermark). Very small opt-in sample (46) of IIoT adopters; perceived benefits only; the abstract-level screening note ('survey of Italian manufacturing companies') overstated the evidence. Low weight for RQ4; keep mainly as an example of self-reported TBL effects of an I4.0 technology.

authors: Cagno, E.; Accordini, D.; Neri, A.; Negri, E.; Macchi, M.
title: Digital solutions for workplace safety: An empirical study on their adoption in Italian metalworking SMEs
population: Employers of Italian metalworking SMEs (mainly NACE C25, Lombardy 70%); questionnaire distributed by ApiTech (Confapi digital innovation hub) and IAL; 188 SMEs
ai_definition: Adoption of digital solutions for occupational safety (wearables such as smartwatches, smartphones, cameras, environmental sensors, exoskeletons, etc.) mapped to hazardous situations; three states: adopted/adopting, interested/evaluating, not interested. No AI-specific item.
coi_note: Academic authors (Politecnico di Milano); data collected by ApiTech/Confapi and IAL (CISL-linked training body), anonymised before analysis; no vendor.
notes: Full text read (publisher PDF, Wayback copy of the Politecnico di Milano IRIS file; PDF pages 1-20 correspond to the article pages). Narrow scope: digital solutions for occupational safety, not AI; relevant for RQ3 as a barrier profile of micro and small metalworking firms (lack of perceived benefit, privacy, cost) and as evidence of a low digital base (67% low digitalisation). Adoption percentages by hazard (Table 7) are an image and are not quoted. Convenience sample through an employers' association; fieldwork dates not stated.

authors: Capestro, M.; Di Maria, E.; Bettiol, M.
title: Exploiting Industry 4.0 beyond expectations: an empirical study of manufacturing firms
population: Italian manufacturing firms in the Made in Italy sectors (automotive, furniture, home products, fashion) located in Northern Italy; AIDA population of 7,714 firms; 1,229 respondents (15.9 per cent response rate); analysis on the 168 firms adopting at least one of seven I4.0 technologies (32.7 per cent micro, 42.3 small, 19.6 medium, 5.4 large by turnover class)
fieldwork_period: 2017 (CAWI followed by CATI), immediately after the launch of the National Plan Industry 4.0
ai_definition: Binary use of seven Industry 4.0 technologies (advanced robotics, additive manufacturing, laser cutting, big data/cloud, 3D scanners, augmented reality, IoT); breadth = number adopted (1-7). AI not asked; big data and cloud are merged in a single item.
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova); no conflict declared.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). SEM on the 168 Industry 4.0 adopters within the 2017 Padova CAWI/CATI survey of Northern Italian Made in Italy manufacturers (population 7,714 from AIDA, 1,229 respondents, 15.9 per cent response rate; data refer to 2016-2017, so 'date' lowered to 1). The abstract-based guess that this is the same 2017 Padova survey as bettiol2022ict and bettiol2023collaboration is confirmed. AI is not measured: the seven binary technology items merge big data and cloud, and the model uses only the count of technologies (breadth, mean 2.21). The headline Italy-specific figures are the implied 13.7 per cent of respondents adopting at least one technology and, among adopters, 43.5 per cent using big data/cloud, 44.0 per cent advanced robotics and 23.8 per cent IoT. Limitations: non-probability, adopter-only analysis, self-reported binary outcomes with low reliability (alpha 0.513-0.670), cross-sectional, Northern Italy only. Relevance: RQ1 (early adoption and technology mix in Northern Italian SMEs, 2017), RQ2 (market vs production motives and outcomes), RQ3 (market orientation and firm size as drivers of breadth), RQ4 (self-reported outcomes, no causal design), RQ5 (same survey reused across several Padova papers, which inflates apparent source count).

authors: Coco, N.; Colapinto, C.; Finotto, V.
title: Fostering digital literacy among small and micro-enterprises: digital transformation as an open and guided innovation process
population: 74 micro, small and medium enterprises (47 per cent micro, 41 per cent small, 12 per cent medium; 85 per cent family firms; 24 per cent manufacturing, the rest trade and services) in the provinces of Venice and Rovigo, selected by the Chamber of Commerce for the Punto Impresa Digitale (PID-VeRo) initiative
geography: Veneto (provinces of Venice and Rovigo), Italy
fieldwork_period: December 2018 call; action research January to September 2019; follow-up survey May 2023
ai_definition: No AI measure. Digital maturity assessed with the Chambers of Commerce SELFI4.0 self-assessment (68 questions, 7 dimensions: accounting, markets and clients, IT, HR, sales, logistics, technologies for operations), yielding five maturity levels (beginner, apprentice, specialist, expert, champion); adoption of Industry 4.0 technologies treated qualitatively through interviews and workshops.
coi_note: Authors (Ca' Foscari and Bologna) designed and ran the PID-VeRo initiative they evaluate, funded by the Chamber of Commerce of Venice and Rovigo; no financial conflict declared, but the evaluation is of their own intervention.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Action research (two cycles, January-September 2019, plus a May 2023 follow-up with about 50 per cent attrition) on 74 MSMEs of the Venice and Rovigo provinces selected by the Chamber of Commerce for the Punto Impresa Digitale programme; only 18 firms (24 per cent) are manufacturers, so manufacturing_coverage is corrected from none to sector_breakdown_incl_manufacturing and geography is Veneto, as suspected. AI is not measured anywhere; digital maturity comes from the Chambers' SELFI4.0 self-assessment and AI appears once as a topic a respondent would like future training on. The abstract-based coding was not wrong but incomplete. Limitations: purposive non-random sample, authors evaluate their own intervention, self-reported follow-up on half the firms, no comparison group. Relevance: RQ3 (barriers in family MSMEs: inertia, identity threat, generational succession, skill scarcity, fear of wrong investments, preference for subsidies over transformation; enablers: Chamber of Commerce PID network, university mentoring, design thinking, peer networks), RQ5 (illustrates how institutional self-assessment tools like SELFI4.0 define 'digital maturity' without an AI item).

authors: De Giovanni, P.; Belvedere, V.; Grando, A.
title: The Selection of Industry 4.0 Technologies Through Bayesian Networks: An Operational Perspective
population: Italian manufacturing firms and service firms directly involved in manufacturing (logistics, ICT and engineering consulting) adopting or considering Industry 4.0 technologies; 289 usable questionnaires: 22% small (<50 employees), 33% medium (50-250), 45% large (>250); respondents mainly operations (39%), supply chain (16%) and top management (15%)
fieldwork_period: not stated (manuscript received May 2022; technology list refers to the 2016 National Industry 4.0 Plan)
ai_definition: AI not measured. Seven Industry 4.0 technologies taken from the National Industry 4.0 Plan list (IoT, cloud computing, robotics, AGV, 3-D printing, big data, digital supply chain), each with a self-declared level of adoption; operational performance (quality, time, flexibility, efficiency, servitization, sustainability) is the respondent's 1-5 rating of how much I4.0 improved it. AI is explicitly left to future research.
coi_note: Academic authors (LUISS, Cattolica Milano, SDA Bocconi); no funding or conflict declared; analysis run in the commercial package BayesiaLab 9.1.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Questionnaire survey (period not stated; published online September 2022) of 289 Italian manufacturing and manufacturing-related service firms, skewed to large firms (45% over 250 employees) and to operations managers; adoption of the seven National Industry 4.0 Plan technologies (IoT, cloud, robotics, AGV, 3-D printing, big data, digital supply chain) is linked to self-rated 1-5 improvements in six operational performances through a Bayesian network learned in BayesiaLab with what-if (hard evidence) analyses. AI is NOT measured: it is explicitly listed among technologies left for future work, so the paper informs the I4.0 bundle rather than AI. Limitations: self-selected sample of adopters (only 2% without any I4.0 technology), perceived rather than measured performance, no fieldwork dates, response rate not reported, joint-probability tables are images not captured in the text layer (only AGV 0.40 and robotics 0.63 are quoted in prose). The abstract-based coding was correct but incomplete: the full text gives size and sector shares and many effect sizes. Relevance: RQ4 (perceived operational effects of I4.0 technologies, strongest for AGV/robotics on efficiency and time, weak and limited to big data for sustainability, none for quality) and RQ5 (illustrates how Italian I4.0 surveys measure perceived improvement among incentive-driven adopters, not comparable with institutional AI adoption rates); marginal for RQ1 (adoption probabilities within an adopter sample) and RQ3 (incentive-driven adoption as a risk).

authors: Battistoni, E.; Gitto, S.; Murgia, G.; Campisi, D.
title: Adoption paths of digital transformation in manufacturing SME
population: Manufacturing SMEs in Tuscany with positive economic performance in the previous three years, in six regionally selected traditional and district sectors (apparel 51%, machinery 23%, boat building and furniture 11%, chemicals 5%, jewellery 5%, paper 5%); sampling frame 2,741 SMEs; 421 completed interviewer-administered questionnaires (15.36%); 22% micro, 61% small, 17% medium
ai_definition: No AI adoption rate. Digital technologies associated with Industry 4.0 classified into four hierarchical layers (Sensor 12 items, Integration 9, Intelligent 7, Response 12) measured as formative indexes from 5-point items on data collection, integration, processing (analysis of purchasing, sales, post-sales, marketing, R&D and maintenance data by 'reliable tools') and use; the Intelligent layer is described as big data analysis, artificial intelligence and forecasting of operational and market data. PLS-SEM plus Necessary Condition Analysis.
coi_note: Academic authors (Tor Vergata, Siena); survey funded by the Tuscany Region (POR FESR project STIA 4.0). No commercial interest.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Interviewer-administered survey of 421 Tuscan manufacturing SMEs (frame 2,741 profitable SMEs in six regionally chosen district sectors, 15.36% response, July 2018 to October 2019), analysed with PLS-SEM (5,000 bootstraps) and Necessary Condition Analysis to test whether the Sensor, Integration and Intelligent layers of Lu and Weng (2018) are should-have and must-have factors for the upper layers. AI is not measured as a separate adoption item: it is conceptually part of the Intelligent layer (big data analysis, AI, forecasting), whose seven survey items ask whether purchasing, sales, post-sales, marketing, R&D and maintenance data are 'validated and analysed' by 'reliable tools'; no adoption rates by technology are reported, only latent-score relations. Headline results: Sensor -> Integration 0.755, Integration -> Intelligent 0.508, Intelligent -> Response 0.201 (all p<0.001); NCA shows Sensor is a large necessary condition for all upper layers (d 0.34-0.44) and Intelligent technologies are 'still limited' in SMEs; paths invariant across micro, small and medium firms and across sectors. Limitations: single region with the lowest I4.0 advancement per MISE 2018, profitable SMEs only, formative indexes without descriptive adoption percentages, cross-sectional. Relevance: RQ1 (depth: the AI/analytics layer sits on a weak sensing and integration base in Italian SMEs), RQ3 (data infrastructure as enabler, policy sequencing), RQ5 (layer-based operationalisation versus technology checklists).

authors: Bettiol, M.; Capestro, M.; Di Maria, E.; Grandinetti, R.
title: Leveraging on intra- and inter-organizational collaboration in Industry 4.0 adoption for knowledge creation and innovation
population: Italian manufacturing firms (Made in Italy sectors, mostly northern Italy); CAWI survey of about 1,400 firms, of which about 200 I4.0 adopters; cleaned sample of 137 adopters
ai_definition: Breadth I4.0 = count (1-7) of technologies adopted among autonomous robots, additive manufacturing, big data/cloud, augmented reality, IoT and smart products, laser cutting, 3D scanners; depth I4.0 = count (1-7) of value chain activities where they are used. AI not a separate item.
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova).
notes: Full text read (Emerald OA PDF via Wayback; vol. 26 no. 7, pp. 328-352; printed page = PDF page + 327). Adopters-only analysis (137). Useful as a depth measure for RQ1: adopters use on average 2.4 technologies in 2.5 value chain activities (out of 7). The 2017 fieldwork coincides with the first year of the Industry 4.0 Plan. Effects are self-reported Likert outcomes (knowledge creation), cross-sectional, PROCESS mediation with bootstrap; not causal. Firm size correlates with breadth and collaborations but not with knowledge creation.

authors: Pedota, M.; Grilli, L.; Piscitello, L.
title: Technology adoption and upskilling in the wake of Industry 4.0
population: Italian firms with at least 10 employees in NACE C-N (excl. K) and S95.1, from the ISTAT/Eurostat ICT in enterprises survey 2018 (census of 250+ employees, stratified random sample of 10-249); 21,934 firms
fieldwork_period: ISTAT ICT survey 2018; technology investments refer to 2016 and 2017; upskilling to 2017
ai_definition: Adoption = firm invested in the technology in both 2016 and 2017, for six I4.0 technologies: augmented reality, big data analytics, cloud computing, IoT, advanced robots, 3D printing (ISTAT ICT survey items). No AI item. Factor analysis yields a 'digital' (AR, BDA, cloud) and a 'physical' (3D printing, robots) adoption propensity.
coi_note: Academic authors (Politecnico di Milano); ISTAT microdata.
notes: Version read: accepted manuscript deposited in the Politecnico di Milano repository (48 pages, tables at the end; obtained through a Wayback Save Page Now capture because the repository blocks direct downloads). Page numbers refer to the preprint PDF (printed page numbers coincide with PDF pages), not to the TFSC article (vol. 187, 122085). Important for RQ5: same ISTAT ICT-in-enterprises frame as istat2025ict but adoption is defined as investment in both 2016 and 2017 and figures are unweighted counts, so the 19% adopter share (4,223/21,934, own computation) is not comparable with ISTAT's weighted published rates. Manufacturing is included with sector dummies but results are not broken down by sector. Cross-sectional, correlational.

authors: Aldrighetti, R.; Battini, D.; Das, A.; Simonetto, M.
title: The performance impact of Industry 4.0 technologies on closed-loop supply chains: insights from an Italy based survey
population: Companies (mostly manufacturing, plus construction/environmental services and transport/logistics) in the regions the authors call north-east Italy (Lombardia, Emilia Romagna, Veneto), Confindustria contact lists, no sector restriction; 887 firms e-mailed, 96 completed responses (10.8%), of which 55 CLSC adopters and 81 I4.0 adopters; PLS-SEM run on the 51 (elsewhere stated 55) firms jointly adopting CLSC practices and I4.0 technologies in the previous five years
geography: Italy, northern regions (Lombardia, Emilia Romagna, Veneto); not nationally representative
ai_definition: Artificial intelligence is a separate item (I4.0_ADO13) among 13 I4.0 technologies: respondents rate, for each technology, the share of their I4.0 investment (0 = not invested, 1-5 Likert) and the investment duration (0-5 years). The questionnaire defines AI as 'advance computer systems that elaborates data and functions following human behaviour' with consumer examples (Siri, Cortana, chatbots). In the measurement model AI is grouped with the process-driven technologies (CPS, additive manufacturing, AR, VR, cobots), although the literature section lists it among data-driven ones (IoT, big data, cloud, integration software, cybersecurity). No AI-specific adoption rate is reported in the text (only in Figure 5 graphically).
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova, Baruch College, NTNU); funded by the regional ERDF POR 2014-2020 'Closed Loop Supply Chain' project and Fondazione Speedhub; contacts supplied by Confindustria; authors declare no conflict of interest. Findings discussed with project industry partners.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Online opt-in survey (Google Form, 15 April to 27 November 2019) of operations managers in firms from Confindustria lists in Lombardia, Emilia Romagna and Veneto (the authors call this 'northeast'): 887 contacted, 96 completed (10.8%), 57% CLSC adopters, 84% I4.0 investors in the last 5 years; PLS-SEM (SmartPLS, 1,000 bootstraps) on the 51 firms (stated as 55 on p. 13, an internal inconsistency) adopting both CLSC practices and I4.0. AI IS a separate questionnaire item (I4.0_ADO13, investment emphasis 0-5 and duration 0-5), defined for respondents with consumer examples (Siri, chatbots), but no AI-specific adoption rate is given in text (only Figure 5) and the item is grouped with the process-driven bundle in the model (while listed as data-driven in the literature review). Headline results: CLSC -> performance beta 0.720 (p<0.001); composite I4.0 moderation ns (0.123) but direct I4.0 -> performance 0.192 (p<0.05); data-driven I4.0 moderation 0.183 (p<0.05, f2 0.060); no moderated effect on financial performance (0.102 ns), marginal on environmental (0.181, p<0.1; wastes 0.171, p<0.05), significant on social performance (0.198, p<0.05); size, turnover, sector and competitors not significant. Managers report no economic barriers thanks to government incentives, but lack of guidance on which technologies to adopt first and lack of workforce expertise. Limitations: tiny non-probability sample skewed to large firms (36% above 500 FTEs, 44% above 100 million euro turnover), self-reported 7-point performance improvements, cross-sectional, one macro-region, 2019 data. Relevance: RQ4 (self-reported performance effects, financial gains not detectable, data-driven bundle matters), RQ1 (84% I4.0 investors in a large-firm Confindustria sample; adoption by size class), RQ3 (barriers: guidance and skills rather than cost), RQ5 (AI as one Likert item inside a 13-technology investment construct, a measurement choice that hides AI-specific adoption).

authors: Zheng, T.; Ardolino, M.; Bacchetti, A.; Perona, M.
title: The road towards industry 4.0: a comparative study of the state-of-the-art in the Italian manufacturing industry
population: Italian manufacturing companies of all sizes (AIDA database plus authors' mailing list; 960 contacted); 102 respondents in 2020, of which 40 also answered the 2017 wave
fieldwork_period: first six months of 2020 (second wave); first six months of 2017 (first wave)
ai_definition: Industry 4.0 operationalised as six enabling technologies (IIoT, big data analytics, additive manufacturing, collaborative robotics, AR/VR, AI); for each, a five-level adoption scale: no knowledge, no action, preliminary study, pilot/implementation, in use. AI is one of the six items.
coi_note: Academic authors (University of Brescia); no sponsor declared.
notes: Full text read (publisher PDF via Wayback copy of the Emerald OA file). Printed page = PDF page + 306 (vol. 30 no. 1, pp. 307-332; online first 2021, print 2023). Non-probability web survey (LimeSurvey), 960 firms contacted, 102 responses (about 10.6%); the sample over-represents large firms and machinery (43.7%). Direct AI figure for RQ1: only 1% of respondents use AI in 2020 and only 26% know it, against 23% for additive manufacturing; this is the lowest-adoption technology of the bundle. Size and information-system coverage are the two significant correlates of the number of technologies adopted. Cost reduction is the main perceived benefit. Figure 2 (adoption levels) is an image; percentages for the other levels are not quoted here.

org: International Journal of Productivity and Performance Management
authors: Bettiol, M.; Capestro, M.; Di Maria, E.; Micelli, S.
title: Disentangling the link between ICT and Industry 4.0: impacts on knowledge-related performance
population: Italian manufacturing firms of Made in Italy sectors in northern Italy (AIDA, 8,022 contacted, 1,400 respondents); analysis restricted to the 206 respondents that adopted at least one of seven I4.0 technologies
fieldwork_period: not stated in the paper (CAWI survey; paper received October 2020)
ai_definition: Binary adoption of seven I4.0 technologies: autonomous robots, additive manufacturing, big data/cloud, augmented reality, IoT and smart products, laser cutting, 3D scanner. AI is not a separate item. ICT base measured as adoption of nine ICT (ERP, CRM, CAD/CAM, CNC, SCM, MRP, web-based tools).
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova, Venezia).
notes: Full text read (Emerald OA PDF via Wayback; vol. 71 no. 4, pp. 1076-1098; printed page = PDF page + 1075; online 2021). Adopters-only sample (206), so no adoption rate for the population; the ratio 206/1,400 (about 15%) is implicit, not stated as a rate. Likely the same 2017 CAWI survey used in bettiol2023collaboration (same seven technologies, same AIDA frame of 1,400 firms), but the fieldwork date is not stated here. Relevant for RQ3/RQ5: prior ICT (especially ERP/CRM) predicts data-oriented I4.0 adoption, consistent with the 'digital base' argument; Operation 4.0 (robots, AR) is linked to B2B markets, not to prior ICT.

authors: Bettiol, M.; Capestro, M.; Di Maria, E.; Micelli, S.
title: SMEs @ Industry 4.0: a comparison between top and average performers
population: Italian manufacturing SMEs in Made in Italy and other industries, split into top performers (stratified sample of 1,986 firms with above-average turnover growth and ROE 2016-2018) and average performers (stratified sample of 4,808 firms); 366 respondents (166 top, 200 average)
ai_definition: Binary yes/no adoption of each of the nine technologies listed in the Italian Industry 4.0 National Plan: advanced robotics, 3D printing, value chain integration systems, big data and analytics, cloud computing, AI, cyber-security, AR, IoT. Adopter = at least one technology adopted.
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova, Venezia); groups defined with a Banca IFIS market report, no bank funding declared.
notes: Full text read (publisher OA PDF, Sinergie vol. 39 no. 3, pp. 27-48; printed page = PDF page + 26). Stratified random samples with CAWI, but low response rates (8.4% and 4.2%) and self-selection bias likely. Useful for RQ1 because AI is an explicit item: 11.9% of top-performer adopters and 7.1% of average-performer adopters report AI, which corresponds to roughly 7% and 3% of all respondents in each group (own computation, not stated in the paper). Cloud is the most adopted technology (52.5% top, 61.2% average among adopters). Top performers adopt more technologies (3+). Motivations: production efficiency first (77.2% vs 60.0%).

authors: Pirola, F.; Cimini, C.; Pinto, R.
title: Digital readiness assessment of Italian SMEs: a case-study research
population: 20 manufacturing SMEs in Lombardy selected by judgmental sampling from a local industrial association (plus 2 in-depth cases); interviews with innovation managers
ai_definition: Digital Readiness Level 4.0 (DRL 4.0): index I (1-5) built from Likert scores on five dimensions (Strategy, People, Processes, Technology, Integration) assessed in about three-hour semi-structured interviews; technology dimension covers HMI, wearables, robotics, additive manufacturing, traceability, cloud. No AI item.
coi_note: Academic authors (University of Bergamo); firms selected through a local industrial association.
notes: Version read: author preprint deposited in the University of Bergamo repository (Aisberg, Wayback copy), 27 pages with tables and figures at the end; page numbers refer to the preprint PDF, not to the JMTM pagination (vol. 31 no. 5, pp. 1045-1083, online 2019). Small judgmental sample of 20 Lombardy SMEs, so no population inference. Useful as a depth/readiness benchmark pre-dating the AI wave: intermediate readiness (2.8/5), weak integration, no cloud analytics. Fieldwork year not stated (likely 2017-2018 given cited sources).

authors: Zheng, T.; Ardolino, M.; Bacchetti, A.; Perona, M.; Zanardini, M.
title: The impacts of Industry 4.0: a descriptive survey in the Italian manufacturing sector
population: Italian manufacturing enterprises and Italian sites of multinationals of any size and sector, selected mainly from AIDA; 956 companies invited, 146 individual responses from 103 companies (56.3% SMEs with revenue below 50 million euro, 28.2% large, 15.5% very large above 300 million; machinery 35%, metal products 16.5%, electrical equipment 13.6%, metals 9.7%, automotive 6.8%)
ai_definition: No AI item. Knowledge (null, superficial, medium, profound) and utilization (no knowledge, not in use, preliminary study, in use) of six Industry 4.0 enabling technologies adapted from the Italian National Plan: IIoT, additive manufacturing, big data and advanced analytics, virtual and augmented reality, cloud manufacturing, collaborative robotics; utilization level classed as null, low (1-2 technologies), medium (3-4), high (5-6). Big data and advanced analytics is the closest proxy for AI.
coi_note: Academic authors (RISE Laboratory, University of Brescia); no sponsor disclosed.
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Descriptive web survey (110 questions, modular by technology) run in the first half of 2017 on 956 Italian manufacturing companies drawn mainly from AIDA; 146 responses from 103 companies (about 11% after telephone follow-up), skewed towards larger firms (56.3% SMEs vs 99% nationally) and towards machinery and metal sectors. AI is not measured: the six-technology list follows the Italian National Plan (IIoT, additive manufacturing, big data and advanced analytics, AR/VR, cloud manufacturing, cobots) and big data and advanced analytics is the only AI-adjacent item, unknown to more than half of the sample. Headline 2017 figures: additive manufacturing in use at 22% and IIoT at 21%, no cloud manufacturing projects, mean 1.8 technologies among adopters (54% only one), majority of SMEs with no I4.0 project versus more than half of large firms with at least one, knowledge median below 0.2 for SMEs vs 0.4 for large firms, HR and controlling barely involved, high investment and missing competences as top barriers for adopters. The abstract-based coding described the instrument as a 'six-technology, five-level' scale: the full text uses four-level knowledge and utilization scales, corrected here. Limitations: opt-in sample, self-reported, descriptive chi-square only, sample larger than national average so results are optimistic, pre-2018 (date score 0). Relevance: RQ1 (baseline I4.0 breadth and depth in 2017, size gap), RQ2 (business functions involved), RQ3 (informatisation, IT function, competences, investment, incentives) and RQ5 (knowledge vs use operationalisation); companion wave of zheng2023road.

authors: Agostini, L.; Filippini, R.
title: Organizational and managerial challenges in the path toward Industry 4.0
population: Italian manufacturing firms of all size classes, random sample of 1,000 firms from the AIDA database; owner or managing director as respondent; 257 usable questionnaires (32.1 per cent small, 33 per cent medium, 34.9 per cent large)
fieldwork_period: not stated; online survey with two reminders, paper received 3 February 2018 (fieldwork presumably 2017)
ai_definition: Count of the nine Italian National Plan Industry 4.0 technologies (industrial IoT, cloud, cybersecurity, big data and analytics, simulation, horizontal and vertical integration, additive manufacturing, advanced manufacturing solutions, augmented reality) adopted or formally planned, as binary items at process/supply-chain level (max 18) and product level (max 9). No AI item; big data and analytics is one of the nine, not reported separately.
coi_note: Academic authors (Padova).
notes: Verified on full text (3 October 2026). Online survey of a random AIDA sample of 1,000 Italian manufacturing firms of all sizes (257 responses, 25.7 per cent response rate, roughly one third each small, medium, large; fieldwork date not stated, before February 2018), with K-means clustering on the count of adopted or planned National Plan technologies, t-tests and negative binomial regressions, plus 15 validation interviews. AI is not measured: adoption is a count over the nine MISE technologies, of which 'big data and analytics' is one, with no per-technology rates reported. The abstract-based coding was wrong on the cluster count: the full text identifies three clusters (12.4 per cent adopters, 38.2 per cent beginners, 49.4 per cent non-adopters), not two. Limitations: cross-sectional, self-reported, adoption and planning merged in the same binary, pseudo R2 of 0.09-0.10, large firms over-represented relative to the Italian population. Relevance: RQ1 (early adoption distribution in Italian manufacturing circa 2017, 12.4 per cent intensive adopters), RQ3 (enablers: digital skills, lean, ICT infrastructure and open innovation as preconditions; HR practices as moderator), RQ5 (the National Plan nine-technology list as the reference measurement frame of the Padova group).

authors: Antonioli, D.; Ghisetti, C.; Mazzanti, M.; Nicolli, F.; Quatrosi, M.
title: "Twin transition" and HRM practices: empirical evidence from Italian firms
population: Italian manufacturing companies with at least 10 employees, stratified by macro-area, sectoral technological intensity and size class (10-49, 50-249, 250+); two CAWI waves (2020 and 2021) run by the company Izi, about 4,600 responding firms per wave
ai_definition: No AI-specific item. DIGIT = 1 if the firm benefited from at least one incentive of the Italian Industry 4.0 plan (proxy for digital practices: sensors, IoT, ICT infrastructure, big data analytics); GREEN = 1 if at least one environmental innovation; TWIN = DIGIT and GREEN. Logit with year, 2-digit sector and NUTS2/NUTS3 fixed effects; correlational, not causal.
coi_note: Academic authors (Ferrara, Milano-Bicocca, Palermo); PNRR/MUR funding; no conflict of interest declared.
notes: Full text read on the version of record (CC BY) retrieved from the Milano-Bicocca repository BOA (publisher site blocks automated download). Page numbers are PDF pages of the online-first file (PDF page = article page + 1); Crossref gives vol. 32 no. 10, pp. 1184-1203. The paper does not measure AI: the digital variable is participation in the Industry 4.0 incentive programme (self-reported benefit from the plan), so the 22% DIGIT share is a policy-uptake proxy, not a technology adoption rate, and the authors flag self-selection into the programme. Useful for RQ3 (HRM practices, STEM skills, R&D, export and age as correlates of joint green-digital adoption; smallness penalises digitalisation specifically) and RQ5 (footnote 2 compares 13.6% twin with 30% of European firms planning twin investments in EIBIS 2021 and about 39% in the INAPP RIL survey). Table 6/7 report N = 8959 while the text says 8952 firms; both figures are in the article. Results are explicitly correlational (firm fixed effects wipe out the effects). Table 1 p.7: DIGIT = 1 for 26% of medium-high-tech, 26% of medium-low-tech and 19% of low-tech firms.

authors: Chiarini, A.
title: Industry 4.0 technologies in the manufacturing sector: Are we sure they are all relevant for environmental performance?
population: Phase 1: 19 operations managers of Italian B2B discrete manufacturers with more than 50 employees, ISO 14001 certified, that had implemented I4.0 technologies; Phase 2: operations managers of 6,000 ISO 14001-certified Italian B2B manufacturers (Accredia database) with more than 50 employees; 492 completed questionnaires, 186 excluded for poor I4.0 implementation, 46 large firms randomly dropped, final 260 (148 large, 112 medium)
fieldwork_period: not stated (Accredia database accessed October 2020; article received January 2021)
ai_definition: No adoption rate. AI is one of seven I4.0 technologies rated on a 7-point agreement scale for its relevance to environmental performance (variable AI). Table 1 defines AI as technology designed to emulate human brain analysis, learning and making assumptions, divided into machine learning and deep learning, with data analytics often based on AI. Respondents self-screened as having implemented I4.0 in the previous 3 years.
coi_note: Single academic author (Verona); no funding or sponsor declared.
notes: Full text read on the publisher version of record (CC BY) retrieved from the Internet Archive capture of the Wiley pdfdirect link (Wiley blocks automated download). Page numbers are PDF pages 1-14; journal pagination is vol. 30 no. 7, pp. 3194-3207. Attitudinal study: figures are perceived relevance of I4.0 technologies for environmental performance, not adoption rates; the only diffusion figures are the MISE 2018 size breakdown quoted as a sampling benchmark. Sample restricted to ISO 14001-certified B2B discrete manufacturers with more than 50 employees that self-declared fair or good I4.0 implementation; small firms excluded by design; response rate 492/6,000 = 8.2% (computed) before exclusions. Relevant to RQ2 (AI and analytics as the second most relevant I4.0 technology for environmental management, used for pattern finding, prediction and energy reduction) and RQ3 (lack of customised AI software, lack of internal competence, scepticism). Comment counts (14, 4, 19, 8 respondents) are from the author's reading of open-ended comments.

authors: Horvat, D.; Heimberger, H.; Jaeger, A.; Lerch, C. M.
title: The innovation payoff of AI in production: evidence from German manufacturing
population: German manufacturing firms with 20 or more employees, NACE Rev. 2 divisions 10-33 (German Manufacturing Survey 2022, German part of the European Manufacturing Survey); gross random sample of 15,299 sites, net sample 14,045, 1,334 valid questionnaires (10% response rate); respondents = production managers, CTOs or CEOs; multivariate models on n of about 970 (all firms) and about 430 (product innovators)
fieldwork_period: fall 2021 to spring 2022 (four months); reference year 2022, innovation window 2019-2022
ai_definition: AI adoption in production = binary indicator: firm uses AI-based self-learning software solutions (algorithms that recognise patterns and offer actionable recommendations) in at least one of five production areas: management of production processes, quality control, maintenance of machinery and equipment, management of internal logistics, improvement or innovation of production processes. Scope or intensity of use not measured.
coi_note: Fraunhofer ISI and University of Hohenheim authors; survey run by Fraunhofer ISI itself (institutional interest in the GMS, no commercial sponsor).
notes: Full text read on the version of record (CC BY-NC-ND) retrieved from the Fraunhofer Publica repository (publica/521538) because Taylor and Francis blocks automated download. Online first, 1 August 2026, pages 1-25 in Crossref; page numbers given are PDF pages (PDF page = article page + 1). EU comparator for RQ1/RQ2: AI in production measured on its own, by purpose, in a probability sample of German manufacturers with 20+ employees, with the same firm-size threshold as Bank of Italy INVIND (20+). The paper does NOT report AI adoption by firm size, only product innovation by size (Table 4); depth of AI use is explicitly not measured (binary, at least one of five areas). Comparison with Eurostat: Eurostat counts AI in any business function with a 10+ threshold, so the 16% production-only figure is not directly comparable with the 24.4% Eurostat 2025 figure for German manufacturing. Effects on innovation are cross-sectional associations (authors state causal inference is not possible; excluded observations had slightly higher AI and R&D rates, so ORs are described as conservative). Apostrophes and umlauts in author names normalised in the bib key (Jaeger). Other AI estimates cited by the authors for context (p.13-15): up to 11% in the German electrical equipment industry (Rammer et al. 2022, 2018 data) and about 12% in US manufacturing (McElheran et al. 2024, 2018 data). Product innovators by size, Table 4 p.14: 34% (up to 49 employees), 47% (50-99), 52% (100-499), 75% (500+).
